entries.name: Golden Age Fair-Play
entries.description: Every clue shown to the reader before the reveal; the mystery as an honest game.
entries.principle: The fair-play contract, formalized in the 1920s–30s: the reader must theoretically be able to solve the case from evidence presented in plain sight. The pleasure is a game between author and reader, run through a closed suspect pool where misdirection works by selective emphasis, never by lying.
entries.example: Christie's *The Murder of Roger Ackroyd* and *And Then There Were None* are the summit; Sayers, Carr, and Ellery Queen codified variations. The contemporary revival — Horowitz's *Magpie Murders*, Osman's Thursday Murder Club — proves the contract still sells.
entries.application: Plant the real clue early and bury it under false ones of equal visual weight. Every suspect needs motive, opportunity, and a reason to seem guilty that dissolves on the reveal. Audit the finished draft against the fair-play checklist: could an attentive reader have gotten there?

entries.name: Locked-Room / Impossible Crime
entries.description: A crime that appears physically impossible — until the mechanism is shown.
entries.principle: The trick is always a gap between the scene as perceived and the scene as staged: time, space, or identity has been misread. The solution must feel inevitable in retrospect — an impossible crime explained by an implausible contraption breaks the contract it was built on.
entries.example: Carr's *The Hollow Man* contains the form's famous self-aware "locked-room lecture"; Poe's "The Murders in the Rue Morgue" founded it. Japan's honkaku school — Shimada's *The Tokyo Zodiac Murders*, Yokomizo — kept the pure form alive and reexported it.
entries.application: Design the mechanism first, then engineer the perception error that hides it. Rehearse the reveal aloud: if it needs a diagram and three coincidences, simplify. One misdirection should be architectural (the room itself), one human (who we trust).

entries.name: Closed Circle / Country-House
entries.description: Isolation shrinks the suspect pool to a knowable cast — one of us did it.
entries.principle: The isolation mechanism (island, snowstorm, house party, train) does double duty: it limits suspects to a finite, learnable set, and it applies social pressure that makes every conversation a potential slip. The setting is the constraint engine; hospitality curdling into suspicion is the emotional register.
entries.example: *And Then There Were None* is the terminal version — the circle with no detective and no exit. *Murder on the Orient Express* runs the form on rails; *Knives Out* (film) modernizes it intact, proving the machinery still runs.
entries.application: Choose an isolation device the reader accepts without strain, then map the relationships so every pair in the circle has friction the crime exposes. YA expression: the boarding school and the senior-year clique are the form's native YA habitats (*One of Us Is Lying*) — institutional adults must be plausibly sidelined.

entries.name: Cozy Mystery
entries.description: Violence offstage, community center-stage; order restored by an amateur.
entries.principle: A reassurance contract: the crime disturbs a beloved community and the resolution restores it. Gore, despair, and procedural grind are excluded by design; charm, recurring cast, and the sleuth's civilian specialty carry the series. The stakes are personal and communal, never gruesome.
entries.example: Christie's Miss Marple established the village template. The contemporary boom — Osman's *The Thursday Murder Club* and the craft-and-bakery cozies — shows the form's series engine: readers return for the community as much as the puzzle.
entries.application: Build the recurring world first — the shop, the club, the village — and give the sleuth a trade that plausibly generates cases and insights. Keep death consequential but off-page; the tone contract, once set, cannot be broken mid-series without losing the readership it recruited.

entries.name: Amateur Sleuth
entries.description: An ordinary person pulled into detection — and the two problems that creates.
entries.principle: The form lives or dies on two plausibility problems: access (why is this florist at the crime scene?) and competence (why can she solve what police can't?). The solutions are personal stake and a civilian lens — a specialty that sees what the badge misses.
entries.example: Miss Marple's lens is village human nature; Father Brown's is the confessional. Flavia de Luce's is chemistry. The lineage runs unbroken from Nancy Drew to Pippa in *A Good Girl's Guide to Murder*.
entries.application: Give the amateur a day-job lens that genuinely produces deductions, and make police inadequacy structural (indifference, corruption, jurisdiction) rather than stupidity. YA expression: this is YA mystery's core form — the protagonist's institutional powerlessness (can't subpoena, can't arrest, can be grounded) is not a bug but the source of its native tension and ingenuity.

entries.name: Private Eye
entries.description: The licensed outsider, mediating between the official world and the criminal one.
entries.principle: The PI exists because systems fail: clients bring what police won't touch. The case structure is nearly invariant and endlessly renewable — the client lies, the job widens, and a small errand uncovers a large rot. The PI's independence is the point: answerable to a personal code, not a chain of command.
entries.example: Hammett's Continental Op and Sam Spade built it; Chandler's Marlowe gave it a conscience and a voice; Macdonald's Lew Archer turned it toward buried family history. Grafton, Paretsky, and Mosley re-peopled it; Galbraith's Cormoran Strike keeps it current.
entries.application: Start with the client's lie — what they actually want versus what they hired you for is the first mystery. First-person voice is the form's tradition because the PI's perception *is* the product. Test the code: the best PI plots force a choice between the client, the truth, and the license.

entries.name: Hardboiled
entries.description: Crime writing with the sentiment burned off — violence has weight, prose has calluses.
entries.principle: Born in the pulps as a reaction against the drawing room: crime returned to people who commit it for real reasons, in vernacular American prose. The detective survives on a personal code in a world too corrupt to fix; the plot tours a broken social landscape rather than assembling a puzzle.
entries.example: Hammett's *Red Harvest* and *The Maltese Falcon* are the foundation; Chandler's *The Big Sleep* and *The Long Goodbye* the stylistic summit — read with his manifesto "The Simple Art of Murder." The Black Mask school is the common source.
entries.application: The voice is the discipline: dry, concrete, compressed, similes doing moral work. Violence must cost — physically, morally, cumulatively. Plot looseness is an available choice (Chandler's chauffeur), but only if atmosphere and voice are strong enough to carry what structure isn't holding.

entries.name: Noir
entries.description: No detective required: the protagonist is the perpetrator, the victim, or both.
entries.principle: Distinct from hardboiled, though shelved together: noir's center is the doomed protagonist, not the code hero. The mechanism is want → transgression → spiral: an ordinary person's desire meets one opportunity, one bad choice follows, and the walls close with tragic logic. Fate is the antagonist.
entries.example: Cain's *The Postman Always Rings Twice* and *Double Indemnity* are the purest engine; Thompson's *The Killer Inside Me* moves the camera inside the abyss; Highsmith's Ripley novels run noir logic with the punishment indefinitely deferred — the form's most unsettling variation.
entries.application: Engineer the trap before the prose: what does the protagonist want, what opening appears, and which single choice can never be walked back? Then deny exits honestly — every escape route must close for reasons the reader accepts. The ending owes fatalism, not rescue.

entries.name: Domestic Suspense
entries.description: The threat shares a bed: danger inside marriage, family, and home.
entries.principle: Intimacy weaponized — the person who knows you best is best equipped to destroy you. Dread comes from proximity, and from the gap between a household's public performance and its private reality. Unreliable narration is native here, because marriages are co-authored fictions.
entries.example: du Maurier's *Rebecca* is the form's gothic root; Highsmith grew it in suburbia. Flynn's *Gone Girl* detonated the modern wave — *Big Little Lies*, *The Girl on the Train* — built on alternating POVs and timeline reveals.
entries.application: Structure is the weapon: alternate POVs or timelines so the reader holds knowledge one spouse lacks, and let the dread come from watching them act without it. The form runs on gender scripts — who is believed, who performs, who keeps accounts — interrogate them deliberately rather than inheriting them.

entries.name: Psychological Suspense
entries.description: The mind is the crime scene: perception, memory, and identity under attack.
entries.principle: Tension generated from epistemic doubt — the narrator's account may be wrong, induced, or a lie, and the reader's work is deciding which. Gaslighting, amnesia, obsession, and compromised memory are the standard instruments; the twist must recontextualize honestly, never cheat.
entries.example: Highsmith's *The Talented Mr. Ripley* holds the reader inside a predator's rationalizations; Rendell (and as Barbara Vine) built the British school; Hawkins' *The Girl on the Train* runs the compromised-witness engine; Shriver's *We Need to Talk About Kevin* pushes it to tragedy.
entries.application: Control all information through a compromised consciousness and play fair within it: the truth must be present, misread. On the twist, apply the re-read test — every earlier scene must still parse once the reader knows. YA expression: strong and native (*We Were Liars*) — adolescent memory and self-narration make the form's questions urgent rather than borrowed.

entries.name: Inverted Mystery (Howcatchem)
entries.description: The reader watches the crime; suspense transfers from who to how they're caught.
entries.principle: The killer is known from page one, so the engine becomes dramatic irony: the reader holds the truth and watches the detective close in — or watches the killer's perfect plan develop its one flaw. Complicity is the form's secret weapon; readers protect the criminal they've been made to inhabit.
entries.example: R. Austin Freeman's *The Singing Bone* invented it; Berkeley/Iles' *Malice Aforethought* perfected the novel form; *Columbo* (tv) made it a beloved formula — the pleasure is watching the trap assemble from both sides.
entries.application: Plant the fatal oversight early and in plain sight, then make the detective's discovery of it feel earned, not lucky. Manage sympathy deliberately: how much the reader roots for the killer is a dial, and the ending must settle the moral account the complicity ran up.

entries.name: Police Procedural
entries.description: Investigation as institution: the squad, the process, the paperwork, the luck.
entries.principle: A realism contract — cases are solved the way cases are actually solved: canvasses, warrants, forensics queues, informants, and tedium punctuated by breaks. The protagonist is often collective (the squad), and institutional friction — budgets, politics, careerism — is a native subplot engine, not a distraction.
entries.example: McBain's 87th Precinct novels codified the form; Simenon's Maigret is the great forerunner; Mankell's Wallander exported it as social diagnosis; *The Wire* (tv) is its maximal expression — the procedural expanded to an entire city's institutions.
entries.application: Research real procedure, then compress it honestly — cut the boredom, keep the sequence true. Run multiple cases at different stages to structure time. Let the institution push back: the best procedural antagonist is often the department itself.

entries.name: Forensic Thriller
entries.description: The examiner as detective: the body is the text and the lab reads it.
entries.principle: Evidence chains are the plot spine — each finding unlocks the next scene — and the expert's knowledge grants both access and blind spots. The form's promise is authoritative technical detail; its trap is overclaiming what the science can do.
entries.example: Cornwell's *Postmortem* founded the modern form; Reichs' Temperance Brennan series sustains it; McDermid's *The Wire in the Blood* runs the profiling-adjacent variant with the caveats attached.
entries.application: Verify the science to the level of the Forensics & Investigation collection and let accuracy be texture, not lecture. Balance lab chapters against field stakes — the examiner must leave the morgue. Resist the CSI effect: honest timescales and error rates make better suspense than magic labs.

entries.name: Legal Thriller
entries.description: The lawyer as protagonist; the law as battlefield and maze.
entries.principle: A double game: the case being argued in court and the truth moving underneath it. Discovery, deposition, and motion practice are the investigation beats; the ethics of advocacy — defending the possibly guilty, opposing the possibly innocent — supply the moral engine.
entries.example: Turow's *Presumed Innocent* is the modern template and carries the form's best twist; Grisham's *The Firm* runs the lawyer-in-jeopardy variant at thriller pace; Lee's *To Kill a Mockingbird* is the form's conscience, from outside the genre shelf.
entries.application: Make the client's guilt genuinely uncertain as long as possible — ambiguity is the fuel. Legal procedure must be right enough to convince and compressed enough to move. Remember the form's sharpest truth: the verdict and the resolution are not the same event, and the gap between them is where the ending lives.

entries.name: Courtroom Drama
entries.description: The trial as theater: testimony, cross-examination, and the jury as audience.
entries.principle: Confined to the courtroom, the form runs on verbal combat — cross-examination is its swordplay, and each witness is a scene with a winner. The jury functions as the reader's surrogate, and revelations must arrive through testimony, earned by questioning rather than conjured by surprise witnesses.
entries.example: Traver's *Anatomy of a Murder* is the procedure-honest summit; Christie's "Witness for the Prosecution" the great twist machine; *Twelve Angry Men* (film) inverts the form entirely into the jury room and proves deliberation alone can carry a plot.
entries.application: Sequence witnesses for escalation the way a novelist sequences chapters — each cross should change the score. Ground every reveal in the record: the gasp must come from a question the reader saw being loaded. Verdict timing is pacing's last lever; what happens after it is theme's.

entries.name: Espionage
entries.description: Information as currency, loyalty as fiction, betrayal as intimacy.
entries.principle: The spy story runs on institutionalized moral grayness: everyone lies professionally, and the question is what remains of a self that deceives for a living. The mole hunt is the form's signature structure — an investigation where the suspect pool is your own side and every clue is also a betrayal.
entries.example: le Carré's *Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy* is the bureaucratic pole's masterpiece; Fleming is the romantic pole; Deighton the insolent middle. *The Americans* (tv) runs tradecraft and marriage as the same subject — the form's thesis made domestic.
entries.application: Choose your pole first — romantic (competence, glamour, gadgets) or bureaucratic (files, doubt, committee warfare) — because they obey different physics. Tradecraft texture is the genre's forensics: verify it. Build betrayals as relationships first; the deeper the intimacy, the harder the reveal lands.

entries.name: Conspiracy Thriller
entries.description: One person against a hidden system — and every answer widens the plot.
entries.principle: Paranoia escalation: the protagonist pulls a small thread and each revelation implicates a larger layer, until trust itself becomes the scarce resource. The form's native problem is the protagonist's evidence — they must learn enough to be hunted, but proving it must stay just out of reach.
entries.example: *Three Days of the Condor* and *The Parallax View* (films) fixed the 1970s template; Grisham's *The Pelican Brief* runs it through law; Crichton and Ludlum industrialized the chase variant.
entries.application: Give the conspiracy a mundane, financial, or institutional motive — plausibility collapses when the scheme's upkeep exceeds its payoff. Calibrate the ending deliberately: exposure (hope), futility (noir), or absorption (horror) are the three honest exits, and the whole book should be tuned to the one you choose.

entries.name: Techno-Thriller
entries.description: Hardware, systems, and geopolitics: technology plays the role forensics plays elsewhere.
entries.principle: Rigor about machines and procedures generates the suspense — the reader trusts that the submarine, the virus, or the exploit works as described, and the countdown structure converts technical detail into momentum. Competence is the pleasure; operators, not inventors, are the natural POV.
entries.example: Clancy's *The Hunt for Red October* founded the modern form; Crichton ran its scientific wing; Suarez's *Daemon* updated it for software. The form shades into SF at its leading edge — the sci-fi pack's Extrapolation collection covers that border.
entries.application: Research to the hardware level, then dramatize exclusively through people operating under procedure — briefings are for characters, not readers. Keep one system honestly fallible; perfect technology kills suspense. For near-future speculation beyond current capability, consult the adjacent sci-fi pack rather than improvising.

entries.name: Serial-Killer Thriller
entries.description: The predator/hunter duet — pattern as text, profiling as reading.
entries.principle: The killer's signature turns crime into a legible text the investigator learns to read, structuring the plot as a dark correspondence between two minds. The form carries real ethical freight: victim dignity versus lurid spectacle, and profiler mythology versus its modest real-world validity (see Psychology collection).
entries.example: Harris' *Red Dragon* and *The Silence of the Lambs* built the modern template; *Mindhunter* (tv) dramatizes the methodology's actual origins; Fincher's *Zodiac* (film) is the essential counter-version — obsession without resolution, the form's honest shadow.
entries.application: Decide the POV ethics early: killer chapters grant tension but risk glamorization; withholding them keeps the monster mythic. Let the pattern break be the case break. Keep victims persons, not set dressing — the form's best work is distinguished from its worst almost entirely by this.

entries.name: Heist / Caper
entries.description: Crime as project management: the plan, the crew, the complication, the improvisation.
entries.principle: The reader is enlisted on the criminals' side, licensed by target selection (institutions that can afford it, people who deserve it) and by style. Structure is the genre: assemble the crew (each a skill and a flaw), show the plan, run the execution, and break it with the complication that forces improvisation.
entries.example: Stark's Parker novels are the grim pole — process stripped of charm; *Ocean's Eleven* (film) the comic pole; *The Italian Job* and *Heat* (film) mark the range between. Every entry lives somewhere on the charm–consequence dial.
entries.application: Show the plan just thoroughly enough that deviations register as jolts — the reader must know the blueprint to feel it tear. Make at least one complication human (greed, love, betrayal) rather than mechanical. Set the tone dial early: caper forgives, heist-noir collects.

entries.name: Gangster / Organized Crime
entries.description: Crime as institution: the family, the business, the rise and the fall.
entries.principle: The form runs the tragedy arc — rise, consolidation, decay — on the doubled meaning of "family." Loyalty is the currency and its debasement is the plot; violence functions as policy, priced and reluctant, not spectacle. The protagonist's moral ledger is the true account the story keeps.
entries.example: Puzo's *The Godfather* (and Coppola's films) fixed the institutional-tragedy template; *Goodfellas* (film) the view from the shop floor; *The Sopranos* (tv) added therapy and suburbia; Winslow's Cartel trilogy runs it at geopolitical scale.
entries.application: Chart the ledger scene by scene — each compromise must purchase something specific and cost something specific. Generational structure is the form's natural architecture: what the founder did to build, the heir does to keep, and the difference is the theme.

entries.name: Prison Drama
entries.description: The aftermath institutionalized: a closed society with its own law, economy, and time.
entries.principle: Prison compresses the genre's questions — guilt, dignity, survival, justice — into a total institution where the system itself is the antagonist. Internal economies (contraband, favors, protection) supply plot; the sentence structures narrative time in a way no other form offers.
entries.example: King's *Rita Hayworth and Shawshank Redemption* (and the film) is the hope-pole classic; *A Prophet* (film) the formation-of-a-criminal counter-arc; *Orange Is the New Black* (tv) widened the form's population and tone range.
entries.application: Research institutional detail to procedural-grade accuracy — count, commissary, classification — because texture is credibility here. Use time as the medium: what a year means, what ten mean. The escape plot is optional; the dignity plot is not.

entries.name: Historical Mystery
entries.description: Detection before databases: period constraints restore the pure deductive problem.
entries.principle: Stripping away modern forensics returns the form to golden-age conditions — witnesses, logic, and legwork — while period social structures give the detective distinctive access or distinctive obstacles. The era's own beliefs (humors, spirits, honor) provide built-in misdirection modern settings must contrive.
entries.example: Eco's *The Name of the Rose* is the summit — a Holmes homage carrying a cathedral of theme; Peters' Brother Cadfael and Sansom's Shardlake sustain the form at series length; Carr's *The Alienist* works the moment forensics was being invented.
entries.application: Research period investigation methods first — what could actually be known, by whom — and build the puzzle inside those walls. Let period belief systems misdirect honestly. Run an anachronism audit on knowledge, not just objects: the hardest slips are conceptual.

entries.name: Nordic Noir
entries.description: Scandinavian crime as social autopsy: the welfare state examined through its failures.
entries.principle: The crime is a symptom; the diagnosis is social. The form pairs each case with an institutional failure — immigration policy, abuse hidden by respectability, the market's arrival — examined through a melancholic detective whose private disrepair mirrors the public one. Landscape and light do mood work other forms assign to prose.
entries.example: Sjöwall & Wahlöö's Martin Beck novels founded it as explicit social critique; Mankell's Wallander carried it to the world; Larsson's *The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo* detonated its commercial wave; *The Killing* (tv) fixed its screen grammar.
entries.application: Choose the social wound first and let the case grow from it organically — bolted-on issues read as editorial. Pacing runs slower and interiority higher than Anglo-American procedural norms; trust the weather. The detective's private life is not subplot but thesis.

entries.name: Tartan Noir
entries.description: The Scottish school: black humor, class consciousness, and the city as character.
entries.principle: Hardboiled transplanted to Scotland and transformed by voice — gallows wit as pressure valve, Calvinist guilt as undertow, and an unsentimental class awareness. The Edinburgh/Glasgow duality (genteel surface, hard interior; hard surface, warm interior) gives the school its geography of hypocrisy.
entries.example: McIlvanney's *Laidlaw* founded it; Rankin's Rebus series built its cathedral in Edinburgh; Mina and McDermid extended its range and darkened its questions.
entries.application: The voice carries everything — humor and horror in the same sentence is the school's signature move, and it fails if either is diluted. Place-specificity is non-negotiable: streets, pubs, and class markers must be exact. The detective's cynicism should be earned by the city, on the page.

entries.name: Rural / Outback Noir
entries.description: Crime in emptied country: everyone known, nothing witnessed.
entries.principle: The inversion of urban noir — instead of anonymity, total mutual knowledge; instead of no one caring, everyone remembering. Small economies of secrets replace institutional corruption; the land itself (drought, flood, distance) applies pressure and sets clocks. Community memory is both archive and obstacle.
entries.example: Harper's *The Dry* is the modern template — the town's past and the drought arriving together; Woodrell's *Winter's Bone* runs it through Ozark kinship codes; Johnson's Longmire novels give it a procedural spine.
entries.application: Use environment as clock and pressure — harvest, weather, water. The detective is often a returner, welcome and resented, whose own history is part of the evidence. Let the community's memory dole out the past strategically: in a small place, what everyone knows and no one says is the plot.

entries.name: Medical Thriller
entries.description: Medicine's trust inverted: the healer, the hospital, and harm.
entries.principle: The form weaponizes the most universal vulnerability — being a body in other people's hands. Hospitals function as closed worlds with their own hierarchy and procedure, and the horror runs on inverted trust: the institution or expert sworn to help is the threat, or the only one who sees it.
entries.example: Cook's *Coma* founded the modern form and its signature image; Palmer and Gerritsen sustained it; Preston's *The Hot Zone* (nonfiction) shows the contagion wing's factual pole.
entries.application: Verify clinical detail with the same rigor the techno-thriller applies to hardware — readers include nurses. The whistleblower structure is native: someone inside sees the pattern, and the institution's immune response is the second antagonist. Do-no-harm inverted is the engine; keep the ethics visible.

entries.name: Financial Thriller
entries.description: Money as weapon and maze: making abstraction bleed.
entries.principle: The form's core problem is legibility — derivatives don't point guns — so the craft is converting instruments into human cost and insider knowledge into suspense. The learner-character (new hire, investigator, journalist) is the standard solution: the reader masters the scheme as they do.
entries.example: Lewis' *Liar's Poker* and *The Big Short* (nonfiction) are the factual poles the fiction leans on; Grisham's *The Firm* runs the innocent-inside structure; *Billions* (tv) plays the game as open combat between institution and regulator.
entries.application: Dramatize mechanism through consequence: every abstraction must eventually land on a person losing something real. The paper trail is this form's clue chain — build it with forensic care. Greed arcs corrupt by increments; price each step like the gangster novel prices violence.

entries.name: True Crime (Narrative Nonfiction)
entries.description: Real cases under documentary craft — with the ethics load-bearing.
entries.principle: The nonfiction contract: accuracy, sourcing, and the constant tension between narrative shaping and factual fidelity. The form's central craft problem is "satisfying vs. solved" — real cases resist arcs — and its central ethical one is victim dignity: real people, real grief, no license. Analysis here concerns the published works' craft, never fresh commentary on the cases themselves.
entries.example: Capote's *In Cold Blood* founded the form and every debate about it — its "nonfiction novel" liberties are the standing cautionary study. Rule's *The Stranger Beside Me* adds the writer-inside-the-story problem; McNamara's *I'll Be Gone in the Dark* and the podcast *Serial* define the modern documentary-of-doubt mode.
entries.application: Structure around the investigation or the community, not the killer's mythology. Show sourcing inside the text — the modern reader audits. Where the case is unsolved or contested, make uncertainty the shape of the book rather than forcing closure. The Craft collection's true-crime cluster carries the full ethics toolkit.

entries.name: True-Crime-Styled Fiction
entries.description: Fiction wearing documentary clothes: transcripts, interviews, and the podcast frame.
entries.principle: Borrowed authority — the apparatus of the real (case files, oral-history fragments, episode transcripts) creates intimacy and dread that traditional narration can't fake. The found-form's limits are the discipline: the frame can only know what its documents could plausibly contain, and the absent or mediating narrator is the form's built-in irony.
entries.example: Summers' *Sadie* braids a missing girl's POV with the podcast investigating her — the form's YA landmark; Pessl's *Night Film* builds dread from dossier fragments; Horowitz's *Magpie Murders* runs the adjacent metafictional wing.
entries.application: Commit absolutely to the frame's epistemology — one convenient omniscient slip collapses the authority the form borrowed. Let documents contradict each other; the reader's assembly work is the engagement. YA expression: the strongest current YA mystery current (*Sadie*, *A Good Girl's Guide to Murder*) — the podcast frame gives young protagonists an investigative platform institutional power denies them.

entries.name: The Fair-Play Clue Rule
entries.description: The contract that separates a mystery from a magic trick.
entries.principle: Every clue the detective uses must be shown to the reader before the reveal — visible, if not understood. The reader loses fairly or wins fairly; either outcome builds trust, and trust is what sells the next book. Violations aren't edgy, they're refunds.
entries.example: Christie is the standard; Knox's "Decalogue" and Van Dine's rules formalized it in the Golden Age (as guardrails, not laws). Horowitz's modern puzzles advertise their fairness openly — it's a feature readers shop for.
entries.application: Keep a clue ledger while drafting: every fact the solution needs, with the scene where it's planted. In revision, check each against the reader's plausible attention — a clue shown only in a list of forty objects isn't planted, it's hidden. Fairness is about honest emphasis, not mere presence.

entries.name: Red-Herring Construction
entries.description: Misdirection that plays fair: wrong conclusions from true facts.
entries.principle: An honest red herring is a true fact that supports a false inference — the guilty-seeming suspect really did lie, just not about murder. Lying to the reader (false narration, withheld POV knowledge) is not misdirection, it's breach. Every herring needs its own innocent explanation, payable at the reveal.
entries.example: Christie's herrings resolve with satisfying clicks — each suspicious behavior gets its non-murderous reason. *The Moonstone*'s opium solution retroactively honests an apparently impossible deception.
entries.application: Build each herring three-legged: the suspicious fact, the false inference it invites, and the true explanation held in reserve. At the denouement, pay them all — an unexplained herring is a debt default. Match visual weight: the real clue and the false ones must get equal prose emphasis.

entries.name: Clue Burial
entries.description: Hiding the real clue in plain sight — the mystery's sleight of hand.
entries.principle: The classic burial techniques: the list (the key item among trivia), the emotional eclipse (plant during a scene whose drama absorbs attention), the double-duty object (established for one purpose, meaningful for another), and early placement (readers under-weight chapter two by chapter twenty).
entries.example: Christie buries a critical clue inside an argument scene the reader processes as characterization; Sayers hides method clues inside Wimsey's apparently decorative chatter. The technique is the mystery writer's equivalent of the magician's larger gesture concealing the smaller.
entries.application: Plant the real clue before the crime when possible — pre-crime detail reads as texture, post-crime detail reads as evidence. Use POV attention as the burying medium: the narrator glances past what the reader needs. Test on a beta reader: caught it = too loud; can't find it on re-read = too quiet. Re-read visibility is the calibration target.

entries.name: Staging the Reveal
entries.description: The denouement is theater — solve first, explain second, in front of witnesses.
entries.principle: Poe's original architecture still rules: the solution lands, then the walk-back through the clues shows how it was always there. The gathered-suspects scene survives a century of parody because it works — assembled stakes, public accusation, real-time reactions, and the last-moment turn. The explanation must be shorter than the mystery deserved and longer than the reader expects to need.
entries.example: Poirot's drawing-room reveals are the form's ceremony; *Knives Out* stages one knowingly and plays it straight anyway. Tey's *The Daughter of Time* runs the reveal as pure reasoning, no gathering required — proof the essential element is the walk-back, not the parlor.
entries.application: Sequence the explanation as a second, compressed mystery: eliminate the false solutions in ascending order of plausibility before landing the true one. Give the culprit a reaction beat — denial, collapse, or counterattack. Never explain what the reader already assembled; summarizing their own deductions back at them is the form's deadliest sin.

entries.name: Deduction Chains the Reader Can Follow
entries.description: Brilliance the reader can check is worth double brilliance on faith.
entries.principle: A deduction chain earns astonishment when each link is individually simple — observation, inference, conclusion — and only the speed and combination are superhuman. Chains that rest on specialist trivia (the obscure poison, the rare mud) read as authorial cheating wearing the detective's coat.
entries.example: Holmes reading a stranger's history off a hat works because each step is checkable; the famous failures are the trivia deductions. Tey builds an entire novel from documents the reader sees in full — the purest extended chain in the genre.
entries.application: Draft each chain backwards from the conclusion, then audit every link: could an attentive reader make this step with what's on the page? Give the chain one wrong turn corrected mid-course — infallibility reads as authorial hand, fallibility as method. Let the companion ask the reader's questions at the reader's pace.

entries.name: Alibi Construction and Breaking
entries.description: The unbreakable alibi is a promise: the breaking will be worth it.
entries.principle: An alibi puzzle is a time-and-space machine: the culprit appears provably elsewhere, and the solution relocates them by exposing the mechanism — clocks, witnesses, impersonation, or the assumption that the crime happened when it seemed to. The best alibi tricks attack the *when*, not the *where*.
entries.example: Christie repeatedly moves the time of death rather than the suspect; Freeman Wills Crofts built a whole career on timetable alibis and their demolition. The Japanese social school (Matsumoto's *Points and Lines*) made the railway alibi a national art form.
entries.application: Build the alibi from the culprit's plan outward — they designed it, so it must be clever in character for them. Give it one dependency the culprit couldn't control (a witness's habit, a clock's keeper, a schedule change). The detective's break should reframe evidence the reader saw and accepted at face value.

entries.name: POV Strategy: Watson, Detective, or Killer
entries.description: Who narrates determines what mystery you can tell.
entries.principle: The Watson device lets readers feel smart (ahead of the narrator, behind the detective) while keeping the detective's mind offstage where it can dazzle. Detective-POV trades dazzle for interiority and demands the clues arrive fairly through one mind. Killer-POV converts the mystery to inverted form. Multi-POV (Collins' heritage) assembles truth from partial accounts. Each choice is a different contract; changing mid-book breaks all of them.
entries.example: Doyle perfected the Watson; French's Dublin Murder Squad runs damaged detective-POV where the narrator's blind spots are the second mystery; *Gone Girl* weaponizes dual POV itself as the twist mechanism.
entries.application: Choose by asking what the reader must not know and who can honestly not know it. A Watson needs a reason to be present and a temperament worth the pages. If detective-POV, the detective's wrong theories must be genuine — privileged narration that coyly withholds reads as cheating.

entries.name: Suspense vs. Surprise
entries.description: Hitchcock's bomb: fifteen seconds of shock, or fifteen minutes of dread.
entries.principle: Surprise withholds (the bomb goes off unannounced); suspense informs (the audience sees the bomb, the characters don't, and the conversation about baseball becomes unbearable). Mystery runs on managed ignorance, thriller on managed knowledge — and most crime fiction fails by picking the wrong tool for the scene, not by executing badly.
entries.example: Hitchcock's formulation (the bomb under the table) is the craft's most quoted lesson. The inverted mystery is the principle industrialized: *Columbo* gives you the murder and sells you the catching. Christie's *And Then There Were None* alternates the tools chapter by chapter.
entries.application: Scene by scene, decide which the reader should hold: less knowledge than the characters (mystery), more (suspense), or exactly as much (identification). Give away information whenever the dread it buys exceeds the shock it costs — the exchange rate usually favors suspense, and beginning writers usually hoard.

entries.name: Interrogation and Interview Scenes
entries.description: Two people at a table, and everything at stake: the genre's core scene, done right.
entries.principle: An interview scene is a negotiation over information disguised as a conversation, and it must be a scene — both sides want something, both deploy tactics, and the power balance shifts at least once. The witness who simply delivers facts is a database, not a character; what they omit, reshape, or trade is where the scene lives.
entries.example: *The Wire*'s interrogations are tactical set pieces with legality as the net; le Carré's Smiley interviews are chess played with silences; Mina and French write interviews where the detective's own damage is a tool and a liability at the table.
entries.application: Give every interviewee an agenda beyond the questions — protecting someone, deflecting blame, enjoying attention, negotiating leverage. Write the subtext ledger before the dialogue: what each party knows, wants, and will lie about. End on an exchange that changes the case or the interviewer; a scene that only confirms is a summary wearing quotation marks.

entries.name: Twist Architecture and the Re-Read Test
entries.description: A twist is a second story that was always true.
entries.principle: The twist recontextualizes: every prior scene must still parse — and ideally parse *better* — once the reader knows. The re-read test is the gold standard: on second reading, planted evidence should be visible, narration should prove technically honest, and character behavior should be consistent with the hidden truth. A twist that requires the book to have lied is a collapse, not a reveal.
entries.example: *The Murder of Roger Ackroyd* survives its notorious device because the narration is scrupulously, verifiably honest on re-read. *Gone Girl*'s midpoint reversal converts its first half into a different, darker document without invalidating a sentence of it.
entries.application: Write the true version of events first, complete; then draft the surface version over it, checking each scene against both. Audit narration for technical honesty — omission is legal, false statement is not. Budget one twist per structural position; stacked twists devalue each other unless each deepens rather than replaces.

entries.name: Pacing an Investigation
entries.description: The rhythm problem: investigations are repetitive, novels can't be.
entries.principle: An investigation is structurally a loop — question, lead, interview, dead end, repeat — and the craft is disguising the loop as escalation. The standard instruments: rotate scene types (interview, physical evidence, research, confrontation), make each dead end cost something, and let the personal plot advance when the case stalls, so no chapter is only treading water.
entries.example: McBain paces by running multiple cases at different stages; French paces by braiding the detective's private unraveling into the case's rhythm; Christie keeps loops short and ends each with a small recontextualization.
entries.application: Chart the case as an information curve: something the reader values must change every chapter — a fact, a suspicion, a relationship, a cost. When the case must stall for realism, spend the stall on character or dread. The mid-book sag is the form's known failure point: schedule a body, a betrayal, or a reversal for it in outline.

entries.name: Procedural Authenticity vs. Momentum
entries.description: Research is a seasoning, not a course.
entries.principle: Accuracy buys trust; excess detail spends it. The working rule: procedure appears on the page when it creates pressure, conflict, or character — the warrant that won't come, the lab backlogged for weeks, the chain-of-custody error that kills a case. Procedure that merely demonstrates research is a lecture wearing a badge.
entries.example: *The Wire* dramatizes paperwork as institutional combat; Crais and Connelly compress real procedure to its pressure points; the "CSI effect" is the cautionary opposite — fantasy labs that broke a generation of jury expectations.
entries.application: Research twice what you use; use a tenth of what you know. Convert every procedural fact into an obstacle or a cost before admitting it to the page. Where reality is slow (DNA turnaround, warrants), either make the delay a plot pressure or compress it silently — never explain the compression.

entries.name: Dual-Timeline Reveals
entries.description: Then and now, converging: structure as suspense engine.
entries.principle: The dual timeline runs a past thread (the events leading to the crime) against a present thread (the investigation or aftermath), and the suspense lives in the gap — the reader assembles the collision before either thread reaches it. The timelines must trade information asymmetrically: each should recontextualize the other at regular intervals, not merely alternate.
entries.example: *In the Woods* runs a cold childhood case under a present murder; *Big Little Lies* narrates toward a death withheld even in identity; Moriarty and Flynn made the structure the suspense form of the 2010s.
entries.application: Give each timeline its own complete arc and its own mystery — a past thread that exists only to feed the present reads as delivery mechanism. Sequence the handoffs so revelations alternate: past answers a present question, present reframes a past scene. Land the convergence before the ending; the finale belongs to consequence, not chronology.

entries.name: Planting and Payoff Discipline
entries.description: Chekhov's gun, audited: the mystery is the genre of kept promises.
entries.principle: Crime fiction runs a stricter promissory economy than any other genre: every planted object, skill, wound, and relationship is a debt the ending must service, and every payoff must trace to a visible plant. The reader is auditing — that's the game they came to play — so unfired guns and unplanted firings are both breaches of the same contract.
entries.example: Christie's economy is total: examine any of her endings and nearly every element traces backward to a plant. Stark's Parker novels run the criminal version — every tool and flaw established in the plan chapter discharges in the execution.
entries.application: Keep a two-column ledger in revision: plants without payoffs (cut or fire them) and payoffs without plants (plant or cut them). Distinguish texture from promise — a described object becomes a promise when prose emphasis falls on it, so control your emphasis. The skill a protagonist demonstrates in chapter one is the ending you've committed to.

entries.name: The Ticking Clock
entries.description: Deadline pressure, built honestly: time as the antagonist's ally.
entries.principle: A clock converts investigation into race: the next victim, the statute, the trial date, the bomb. Honest clocks obey three rules — the deadline is fixed early and publicly, the consequence of missing it is concrete, and the clock actually runs (progress is measured against it scene by scene). Clocks that stretch when convenient teach the reader to ignore them.
entries.example: *The Day of the Jackal* runs the form's purest clock — the summit date is fixed, and both hunter and assassin move against it; *The Silence of the Lambs* hangs its clock on a named victim in a pit, making the deadline a person.
entries.application: State the deadline in scene, attach it to a face, and reference the remaining time at every act turn. Let the protagonist spend the clock — shortcuts taken under time pressure should create the errors the third act pays for. If the clock must extend, the extension must cost more than the original deadline would have.

entries.name: Stakes Escalation Ladders
entries.description: Rising stakes are built, not declared.
entries.principle: Escalation is a ladder of concreteness: danger moves from strangers to acquaintances to loved ones to self, from livelihood to liberty to life, from private to public. Each rung must be occupied by a specific person or loss the reader has met — "the city is at risk" moves no one; "the sister who lent him the car is now a suspect" moves everyone.
entries.example: Harlan Coben's suburban thrillers climb the ladder rung by rung — each secret exposed endangers someone one step closer to home; *Breaking Bad* (tv) is the long-form masterclass, escalating by consequence accumulation rather than villain inflation.
entries.application: Map the protagonist's attachments before drafting; the plot's job is to walk the threat down that list in order of intimacy. Escalate by consequence, not body count — the tenth corpse is quieter than the first lie to a spouse. Reserve the final rung: the protagonist's own moral line, crossed.

entries.name: Villain POV Management
entries.description: The antagonist's chapters: tension bought with glamorization risk.
entries.principle: Villain POV buys dramatic irony (the reader sees the trap closing) and costs mystery (whodunit dies on contact) and moral framing (inhabited minds attract sympathy — the form's known hazard). The middle instruments: the unidentified villain POV (tension without identity), the letter/interlude, and the strictly rationed glimpse.
entries.example: Harris' Dolarhyde chapters in *Red Dragon* are the form's summit — full interiority that generates horror and pity without excusing; the anonymous killer-POV interludes of the 90s serial-killer boom became cliché through ration failure. Highsmith runs the limit case: Ripley's POV entirely, sympathy fully weaponized.
entries.application: Decide what the villain chapters buy that no other tool can, and ration accordingly — scarcity preserves menace. Keep the POV honest but not omniscient about their own pathology. If the villain is the twist, their POV must pass the re-read test under their true identity.

entries.name: Action Scene Clarity
entries.description: Violence the reader can follow: choreography, geography, and cost.
entries.principle: Action fails as spectacle and succeeds as consequence: the reader must know where everyone is, what each combatant wants beyond survival, and what the outcome changes. Crime-fiction violence carries an extra duty — it should be fast, ugly, and expensive, because the genre's realism contract extends to its fights.
entries.example: Lee Child's fights are taught as physics lessons — Reacher explains the mechanics, which slows time and builds inevitability; Stark writes violence in flat declaratives that make it feel like accounting; *Heat*'s street battle (film) is the choreography-and-geography standard.
entries.application: Establish the geography before the first blow — the reader choreographs with only what you've given them. One action per sentence during combat; compound sentences blur. Every fight must end with a changed situation, a new injury that persists, or knowledge gained; a fight that returns to status quo was a delay, not a scene.

entries.name: Cliffhanger and Chapter-Turn Discipline
entries.description: The page-turn economy: propulsion without cheap tricks.
entries.principle: The honest cliffhanger raises a question the next chapter must actually address; the cheap one manufactures peril that dissolves in the first paragraph after the turn. The sustainable instruments: the revelation turn (new fact recontextualizes), the decision turn (character commits), and the arrival turn (the dreaded thing begins). Fake-outs spend trust at usurious rates.
entries.example: Coben ends chapters on revelation turns almost exclusively — a fact lands, the floor tilts; Corey (in the crime-adjacent Expanse) alternates POVs so every chapter break is also a cliffhanger held in escrow. Patterson industrialized the short-chapter turn; the technique works even when the content thins — which is the warning.
entries.application: End chapters one beat early: write the scene to its natural close, then cut the last exchange and open the next chapter after it. Audit every cliffhanger's cash-out — if the danger evaporates without cost, rewrite the turn as a revelation instead. Vary the turn types; unbroken peril-turns numb by chapter ten.

entries.name: Series Detective Management
entries.description: The long game: keeping a recurring detective alive without embalming them.
entries.principle: The series detective needs continuity (the reader's friend, recognizably themselves) and motion (or the books become reruns). The known strategies: real-time aging (Rankin's Rebus, retirement and all), the frozen clock (Poirot, ageless), the slow arc (Bosch's decades-long institutional souring), and the life-events cadence (Wimsey's courtship). Each trades differently against series length.
entries.example: Rebus ages in real time and the series gains mortality as a theme; Poirot stays fixed and Christie mines variation from structure instead; Connelly lets Bosch's relationship with the institution — not his personality — carry the arc across thirty books.
entries.application: Decide the clock policy in book one; retrofitting age is misery. Give the detective one unresolved private question per book and one per series — the book-level ones close, the series-level one advances by inches. Let supporting cast carry change the detective can't: partners promote, marry, die. The reset-button temptation is strongest after the best book; resist it there especially.

entries.name: Opening Bodies: The Hook and the Discovery Scene
entries.description: The genre's front door: how the crime enters the book.
entries.principle: The opening commits the contract: a body on page one promises pace; a slow domestic overture promises dread; a voice-first opening (Chandler's) promises the sentences will carry. The discovery scene itself is load-bearing — who finds the body, and what that does to them, is characterization the plot will spend later. The corpse should disturb the world of the book, not decorate it.
entries.example: *The Big Sleep* opens on voice and a house, body deferred; Cornwell opens in the morgue, promising procedure; *In the Woods* opens on the old case's dread before the new body lands — three contracts, all kept.
entries.application: Open with the promise your book keeps; a thriller-paced first chapter on a literary-paced novel is a bounced check. Make the discoverer someone the discovery costs. Delay is available — Christie routinely spends two chapters on the doomed household — but only if the delay builds the stakes the body will cash.

entries.name: Humor in Crime Fiction
entries.description: The pressure valve, the scalpel, and the tonal contract.
entries.principle: Humor in crime writing does three legitimate jobs: pressure relief (gallows humor as survival tool — cops and pathologists actually talk this way, so it doubles as realism), characterization (who jokes, when, at what), and social scalpel (comedy as critique, the Tartan school's specialty). The hazard is tonal breach: humor that mocks the victim or defuses stakes the book needs.
entries.example: Leonard's dialogue is the American summit — comedy from character density, never at the corpse's expense; Rankin and Mina run gallows wit as institutional realism; Osman builds whole cozies on charm while keeping the deaths genuinely sad — the tonal needle threaded.
entries.application: Set the humor register in chapter one and hold it; readers forgive dark or light but not lurching. Aim jokes at power, procedure, and the self — never down at victims. In dark material, place humor just before dread, not after: relief that precedes horror sharpens it; relief after dissolves it.

entries.name: Ethics of Writing Real Cases
entries.description: The people are real: the form's first constraint and first principle.
entries.principle: True crime's subjects did not consent to being material. The working ethics: verify everything against sources; distinguish record from speculation on the page; weigh exposure harms to victims' families, the wrongly suspected, and bystanders; and interrogate your own project — is this account serving understanding, or appetite? These constraints are not limits on the craft; in the form's best work they *are* the craft.
entries.example: *In Cold Blood* founded the form and its ethics debates simultaneously — Capote's fabrications and his relationship with the killers remain the standing case study. McNamara's *I'll Be Gone in the Dark* models the opposite pole: obsessive sourcing, victims centered, the investigator's own obsession examined.
entries.application: Build the source spine first — records, transcripts, interviews — and mark every inference as inference in the text itself. Contact ethics: living subjects deserve the chance to speak or decline. Apply the family test to every lurid detail: is it load-bearing for understanding, or decoration for appetite? Cut decoration.

entries.name: Victim Dignity and the Center of Gravity
entries.description: Whose story is it: the structural choice that defines the form's morality.
entries.principle: Every true-crime narrative chooses a center of gravity — killer, investigation, victim, or community — and the choice is ethical as well as structural. Killer-centered accounts risk mythologizing (and feed the market that rewards it); victim- and community-centered structures restore the person the crime erased. The victim as fully rendered life, not biographical garnish before the violence, is the modern form's dividing line.
entries.example: Rule's *The Stranger Beside Me* holds Bundy at center but spends its authority on the women; *I'll Be Gone in the Dark* structures around the investigation and the communities in fear; the podcast era's best work (*In the Dark*) centers institutional failure rather than predator psychology.
entries.application: Render the victim's life with the same narrative investment as the crime — pages, scenes, voice, specificity. Name the killer strategically or minimally; the market's mythology machine doesn't need your contribution. Structural test: if the victim's chapters were cut, would the book still work? If yes, the center of gravity is wrong.

entries.name: Documentary vs. Novelistic Structure
entries.description: The form's central tension: shaped like a story, bound by the record.
entries.principle: Narrative craft (scenes, arcs, reveals, reconstructed interiority) makes true crime readable; the record makes it true. The negotiation is constant: reconstructed dialogue and inhabited perspective import fiction's power and fiction's license, and every borrowing must be either sourced or flagged. The form's history is a history of this line being drawn, blurred, and redrawn.
entries.example: Capote called *In Cold Blood* a "nonfiction novel" and took liberties still being audited; Mailer's *The Executioner's Song* pushed further with a novelist's toolkit on documentary matter; modern practice (Grann's *Killers of the Flower Moon*) shows scene-craft built strictly from citable sources — the contemporary standard.
entries.application: Reconstruct scenes only where sources support every element — dialogue from transcripts and interviews, interiority from the subject's own accounts. Flag the seams honestly ("she later recalled…") rather than laminating over them; visible sourcing is the modern form's style, not its failure. Where the record is silent, write the silence — gaps honestly held are more powerful than gaps filled.

entries.name: The "Satisfying vs. Solved" Problem
entries.description: Real cases don't arc: the form's structural honesty test.
entries.principle: Fiction promises resolution; reality delivers acquittals, cold cases, ambiguous confessions, and doubt. The true-crime writer inherits an ending they cannot improve, and the craft is building a satisfying *book* around an unsatisfying *outcome* — shifting the payoff from verdict to understanding: of the case, the institutions, the community, or the limits of knowing itself.
entries.example: *Serial* season one made irresolution itself the subject and gripped millions; *I'll Be Gone in the Dark* was published before the arrest — its arc is the search, and the postscript history wrote is separate from the book's own completeness; *Zodiac* (film) structures obsession-without-answer as tragedy.
entries.application: Identify what *can* resolve — a question about the institutions, the era, the investigation's failures — and architect toward that, letting the case's factual status be what it is. Never imply certainty the record doesn't hold; the reader's trust is the form's only currency. If the case resolves after publication, your book's integrity is what survives the update.

entries.name: Legal Exposure and the Publication Gauntlet
entries.description: Defamation, rights, and the living: the constraints that shape what can be printed.
entries.principle: True crime is written inside legal walls fiction never touches: defamation (the wrongly-implied suspect is the classic suit), privacy torts, the open-case problem (prejudicing proceedings; sub judice rules outside the US), and rights questions around sources and life stories. These constraints shape structure — what can be alleged, implied, or juxtaposed — and the craft includes writing powerfully inside them.
entries.example: The genre's cautionary files are full of implication suits from secondary figures; publishers legal-read the category as standard practice. McNamara's careful handling of unnamed suspects, and the podcast era's on-air corrections culture, model the working discipline.
entries.application: Treat legal review as a craft stage, not an obstacle: expect it, draft for it, and learn the patterns — assertion vs. attributed allegation, the difference between reporting a suspicion's existence and endorsing it. Keep interview releases and source records. For an ongoing case, know the jurisdiction's rules before structuring the book around material a trial could seal.

entries.name: Podcast-Era Structure and Serialized Doubt
entries.description: The form's newest grammar: episodic investigation, audible uncertainty.
entries.principle: Serial audio rebuilt true-crime structure around the investigating presence: the episodic reveal cadence, the cliffhanger of doubt (each episode revises the last), the host's audible thinking as narrative spine, and the audience as deputized investigators — with all the ethical hazards that deputization brought. Print true crime now inherits readers trained on this grammar.
entries.example: *Serial* built the template; *In the Dark* took it to institutional-accountability journalism of the highest grade; *Sadie* (fiction) and the true-crime-styled novel wave show the grammar's migration into fiction. The web-sleuth disasters that followed some podcasts are the cautionary appendix.
entries.application: Borrow the cadence — chapter-as-episode, each ending on a revision of understanding — where it serves the material. If you write yourself in as investigating presence, your process, bias, and errors become part of the record: narrate them honestly. Do not deputize the audience against living people; the form's worst outcomes all start there.

entries.name: YA Voice and the Limits of Knowing
entries.description: Writing the young detective honestly: what they can know, do, and get away with.
entries.principle: YA mystery's constraint is its engine: the protagonist can't subpoena, interrogate under caution, or access the case file — so investigation runs through social engineering, digital fluency, institutional blind spots, and risk adults wouldn't take. The voice must be genuinely adolescent in judgment and priority — an adult detective in a teen body is the form's most common failure.
entries.example: *A Good Girl's Guide to Murder* builds its whole method from a school project's plausible access; *One of Us Is Lying* runs detection through social knowledge adults can't reach; *Sadie* gives its protagonist the podcast as investigative platform — each solves the access problem in-world.
entries.application: Solve access structurally, once, early: the school assignment, the family connection, the platform. Let adolescent priorities (loyalty, reputation, first love) genuinely compete with the case — that competition is the YA form's real plot. Adult institutions should be obstacles with texture, not cartoons: the police who dismiss her should be right to, procedurally.

entries.name: Institutional Power and the Adult Problem
entries.description: Every YA mystery must answer: where are the grown-ups?
entries.principle: The genre's structural question — why don't the adults handle this? — must be answered honestly or the premise leaks. The load-bearing answers: adults are the threat (the form's darkest wing), adults are captured (the institution protects itself), adults don't believe (credibility gap as engine), or adults are absent by circumstance. "Adults are stupid" is not an answer; it's a leak.
entries.example: *One of Us Is Lying* runs the don't-believe engine — the police theory is plausible and wrong; *Sadie* runs absence and institutional indifference to a missing girl the system deprioritized; boarding-school mysteries run the captured institution protecting its name.
entries.application: Choose the adult-problem answer during premise design and stress-test it: at each plot point, ask what a competent, caring adult would do, and make sure the answer is unavailable for structural reasons. Let one adult be genuinely helpful but insufficient — total adult failure reads as contrivance; partial, well-meant failure reads as the world.

entries.name: Hope, Agency, and the YA Ending Contract
entries.description: Dark material, survivable endings: the form's implicit promise.
entries.principle: YA crime fiction goes dark — abduction, murder, abuse are staples — but the form carries an ending expectation adult noir doesn't: the protagonist's agency must matter, and the conclusion must leave the future inhabitable. This is not a content restriction but a structural one: bleakness is available everywhere except the answer to "did what she did count?"
entries.example: *Sadie* is instructive precisely because it pushes the boundary — its ambiguous ending devastates, but the protagonist's agency drove every event, and the witnessing itself is the hope the book offers; *A Good Girl's Guide* delivers full resolution while permanently costing its heroine her innocence about institutions.
entries.application: Let the protagonist's choices causally drive the resolution — rescue by adult intervention breaks the contract even when realistic. Price the victory honestly: what she learned about her town, her family, herself should cost. Devastation is permitted; futility is not. The reader finishing must believe acting was better than not acting.

entries.name: Content Calibration Without Condescension
entries.description: Writing violence and darkness for younger readers without lying to them.
entries.principle: YA calibration is about camera placement, not subject avoidance: the form handles murder, assault, and grief, but chooses where the lens stands — aftermath over act, emotional consequence over forensic detail, dread over gore. Condescension (sanitizing until stakes vanish) fails the readership as badly as exploitation; teen readers detect both instantly.
entries.example: *The Outsiders* set the standard decades ago — real violence, real death, camera on consequence; *A Good Girl's Guide* handles a murdered girl and an abusive relationship with full seriousness and no lingering; Summers' *Sadie* depicts the aftermath of abuse with a directness that respects readers precisely by not flinching into vagueness.
entries.application: Move the camera, not the subject: the body found, not the killing performed; the funeral, not the wound. Emotional consequence gets full resolution — grief, fear, and anger are where YA spends the realism adult crime spends on procedure. When in doubt, trust the reader's seriousness and doubt your own flinch — vagueness that leaves teens confused about what happened serves no one.

entries.name: Setting as Suspect Pool
entries.description: Where the story happens determines who could have done it.
entries.principle: In crime fiction, setting is casting: the village, precinct, firm, or platform defines the suspect pool, the local law, the surveillance level, and what secrets are worth killing for. The setting's knowledge economy — who sees whom, what's remembered, what's deniable — is the mystery's physics, and it must be designed before the plot, because it determines which plots are possible.
entries.example: Christie's village works because everyone's business is known except the one thing that matters; *The Wire*'s Baltimore determines every case it contains; Harper's drought-struck Kiewarra makes the land itself an accessory. The locked-room is just this principle at maximum compression.
entries.application: Design the setting's knowledge economy explicitly: who observes, who gossips, what's recorded, what's taboo to mention. Match crime to habitat — the fraud belongs to the firm, the poisoning to the family, the disappearance to the empty country. Test: if your plot could happen anywhere, the setting isn't yet doing its genre work.

entries.name: Violence Calibration Across the Genre
entries.description: From offstage cozy death to noir brutality: choosing and holding a register.
entries.principle: The genre spans the widest violence range in fiction — cozy (offstage, consequence only) through classic (discovered, not depicted) through procedural (clinical) through noir and serial-killer work (present, costly) — and register is a contract set in the first chapters. The universal rule across all registers: violence must have weight; the register only determines where the weight lands (community, evidence, psyche, body).
entries.example: Osman kills gently and grieves fully; McDermid depicts hard and makes the depiction the price of the procedural's honesty; Stark writes violence as pure transaction. Each is internally consistent — the failures are the lurches, the cozy that suddenly lingers, the noir that suddenly flinches.
entries.application: Choose the register by asking where you want the weight: on the community (cozy), the puzzle (classic), the institution (procedural), or the body and psyche (noir). Hold it — escalation within register is available, breach is not. Depicted violence should cost the page something: pace, comfort, or a character the reader had plans for.

entries.name: Series Architecture: Standalone vs. Arc
entries.description: The case ends, the series continues: managing two contracts at once.
entries.principle: Every series balances the episodic contract (this book's case resolves — non-negotiable in crime fiction) against the serial contract (lives, institutions, and long threads advance). The working ratios differ by form: cozies run high-episodic, procedurals braid both, and the modern psychological series (French's rotating narrators) reinvents the balance per book. The fatal errors are withholding case resolution to force the next purchase, and resetting so fully that nothing accrues.
entries.example: McBain's 87th Precinct perfected the braid — cases close, the squad's lives compound; French rotates protagonists so each book stands alone while the squad's world deepens; Galbraith runs a five-book romance arc under fully-resolved cases, the modern standard demonstration.
entries.application: Resolve the case, always; the serial threads you may advance, complicate, or cliffhang, but the corpse on page one gets its answer by the last. Plant series threads that compound at different rates — a slow institutional arc, a middle-distance relationship, a fast rivalry. Design book three's debts when writing book one; series that improvise their long arcs read improvised by book four.

entries.name: The Reveal Cascade in Thrillers
entries.description: Sequencing multiple revelations: the endgame's load order.
entries.principle: Modern crime endings rarely fire one reveal; they fire a cascade — and the load order is the craft. The working sequence: solutions before secrets (what happened before what it means), instrumental before emotional (the mechanism before the betrayal), and the recontextualizing reveal last, because whatever fires last is what the book is about. A cascade in the wrong order answers its questions and still lands flat.
entries.example: *Presumed Innocent* sequences verdict, then solution, then the domestic reveal that reframes everything — the order is the meaning; *Gone Girl* fires its cascade at the midpoint and builds a second act on the debris, the structural innovation that made it a phenomenon.
entries.application: List every ending reveal, then order by thematic weight, lightest first — the reader remembers the final recontextualization as the book's statement. Space the cascade across scenes; simultaneous reveals cancel each other. After the last reveal, write the consequence beat: cascades that end the book at the bang leave the meaning unbanked.

entries.name: Fair-Play Audit
entries.description: Run after the full draft: does the mystery honor the contract?
items: Is every fact the solution requires present on the page before the reveal?
Could an attentive reader assemble the solution — in theory — from what's shown?
Does any clue exist only in the detective's head or in specialist knowledge the reader can't access?
Is every piece of misdirection built from true facts and honest emphasis, never false narration?
Does the narration stay technically honest in every scene (omission allowed, lies not)?
Are the culprit's means, motive, and opportunity all established — not just asserted at the end?
Was the culprit on the page early and often enough to be a fair answer?
On a full re-read, does every scene still parse correctly with the solution known?

entries.name: Suspect Viability Checklist
entries.description: For each suspect in the pool — the reveal is only as strong as the alternatives.
items: Does this suspect have a real motive the reader can state in one sentence?
Did they have genuine opportunity — placed at the right time and place on the page?
Do they have a secret or lie that makes them plausibly guilty of *something*?
Does their innocent explanation hold up after the reveal without patching?
Would at least some readers finish the book believing it should have been them?
Are they distinguishable — in voice, want, and function — from every other suspect?
Does suspicion fall on them through story events, not just authorial pointing?
Is at least one suspect more obviously guilty-seeming than the actual culprit?

entries.name: Red-Herring Audit
entries.description: Every false trail, checked for honesty and payment.
items: Is each herring a true fact supporting a false inference — never a lie to the reader?
Does each herring have its innocent explanation held in reserve?
Is every herring paid off — explained — by the final chapter, with no dangling suspicions?
Do the herrings get roughly equal prose emphasis to the real clue (no spotlighting)?
Does at least one herring do double duty — characterization, theme, or subplot — beyond misdirection?
Would cutting any herring change nothing? (If so, cut it.)
Do the herrings point in genuinely different directions, not all at the same decoy?

entries.name: Clue-Plant Tracker
entries.description: The promissory ledger — run in revision, chapter by chapter.
items: List every fact the solution needs; does each have a plant scene identified by chapter?
Is each plant placed before it's needed — ideally before the crime reads as relevant?
Is each plant buried by a legitimate technique (list, emotional eclipse, double-duty object) rather than simply omitted?
Does anything planted with emphasis fail to pay off? (Unfired gun — cut or fire it.)
Does anything pay off without a plant? (Unplanted firing — plant or cut it.)
Are plants distributed across the book, not clustered in a guilty-looking chapter?
Does the protagonist's established skill set match what the ending requires of them?

entries.name: Twist Integrity Check
entries.description: The re-read test, itemized — run before anyone else sees the draft.
items: Written down in one sentence: what does the twist recontextualize?
Does every earlier scene still parse — and ideally parse better — with the twist known?
Is all narration technically honest under the twist (no first-person lies to the reader)?
Is the twist's groundwork visible on re-read without being obvious on first read?
Does the twist deepen the story's meaning, or only its plot? (The best do both.)
Is the character behavior before the twist consistent with the hidden truth?
If there are multiple reveals, does the load order put the most meaningful last?
Could a reader who guessed the twist early still enjoy the book? (If not, the twist is carrying too much.)

entries.name: Procedural-Accuracy Pass
entries.description: For any book touching police, legal, forensic, or medical process.
items: Has every procedural step on the page been verified against a real source, not another novel or TV?
Where reality was compressed (lab timelines, warrants), was it compressed silently and consistently?
Does every procedural detail included create pressure, conflict, or character — not just proof of research?
Are jurisdiction and era right for the procedures shown (PACE vs. Miranda, DNA availability by year)?
Would a professional reader in this field wince at anything? (Find one and ask.)
Are the errors characters make procedurally plausible errors, not idiot-ball moves?
Does the chain of evidence from discovery to conviction hold up if a reader maps it?

entries.name: Series-Detective Consistency Check
entries.description: Run at the start and end of each series book.
items: Is the clock policy (real-time aging vs. frozen) consistent with the previous books?
Are established biography facts, scars, and skills consistent with the series bible?
Does the detective's one series-level question advance by at least an inch?
Does this book's case resolve fully — no withheld corpse-answers to force the next purchase?
Do supporting characters carry change (promotions, losses, arrivals) even where the detective can't?
Could a first-time reader start here and follow everything that matters?
Does the detective's damage stay priced — not reset to zero after last book's cost?
Is anything from earlier books contradicted? (Check the bible, not memory.)

entries.name: True-Crime Ethics & Fairness Checklist
entries.description: For narrative nonfiction and heavily fact-based fiction — run before submission and again at legal review.
items: Is every factual claim traceable to a source you could produce on request?
Is every inference or reconstruction marked as such in the text itself?
Are the victims rendered as full lives, with narrative investment comparable to the crime?
Would the victim's family recognize the account as fair — and have the living been given a chance to speak or decline?
Does any detail serve appetite rather than understanding? (Cut it.)
Are suspicions about named living people reported as attributed allegations, never endorsed implications?
Does the structure center investigation, victims, or community — rather than mythologizing the perpetrator?
Where the case is unresolved, does the book honestly hold uncertainty rather than implying closure?
Has legal review covered defamation, privacy, and open-case exposure for the relevant jurisdictions?
If you appear in the account as investigator, are your own biases and errors part of the record?

entries.name: The Red Herring
entries.description: The false trail built from true facts — misdirection that plays fair.

examples.text: The escaped convict on the moor absorbs suspicion honestly: a real danger, a real secret, and entirely the wrong one.
The "donut hole" structure is herring architecture made visible: the apparent solution arrives early so the real question can hide behind it.
Herrings deployed mechanically: suspicion rotates by spotlight rather than by evidence, so elimination becomes arithmetic instead of deduction.

entries.name: The Least-Likely Suspect
entries.description: The reveal that lands hardest: guilt where the reader's attention wasn't allowed to rest.

examples.text: The terminal version: the culprit hides inside the book's own machinery, and the narration stays technically honest throughout. The standard against which every least-likely reveal is measured.
Solves the problem by exploding it: when every suspect is viable, "least likely" becomes a property of the whole cast.
The cautionary formula: least-likely as mechanical rotation (it's always the janitor/caretaker), teaching that surprise can substitute for fairness. It can't.

entries.name: The Dying Clue
