entries.description: The victim's last message — cryptic by necessity, decoded at cost.

examples.text: Ellery Queen built a career on the device; here the dying message is honestly cryptic: the victim had reasons to encode, not just the author.

examples.work: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo
examples.text: The cold variant: Harriet's diary numbers sit unread for decades, a dying clue whose decoding reopens everything.
Dying clues as weekly puzzle decoration: victims scrawl improbably convenient fragments, and the device's necessity — why encode at all? — goes unasked.

entries.name: The Unbreakable Alibi
entries.description: Provably elsewhere — until the mechanism is exposed.

examples.text: Crofts made the alibi-demolition a form in itself: the timetable examined until the impossible becomes procedural.
Matsumoto's railway alibi is the Japanese social school's signature: the trick lives in a four-minute platform sightline, and breaking it indicts the culprit's institutional world.
Alibi-breaking as weekly formula: mechanisms without motives, ingenuity without consequence — watchable, but it teaches the trick divorced from the story.

entries.name: The Closed Circle of Suspects
entries.description: The finite pool: one of these people did it.

examples.text: The circle sealed absolutely — no detective, no mainland, no exit — and then burned down to zero; the form's outer limit, executed with total nerve.
The honkaku revival's founding homage: a closed circle that knows its Christie and weaponizes the reader's genre literacy against them.
The circle as backdrop: suspects assembled for setting rather than suspicion, with no fair-play machinery underneath the costume.

entries.name: The Loyal Companion Narrator
entries.description: The Watson: ordinary eyes on an extraordinary mind.

examples.text: The archetype: intelligent but consistently one step behind, letting the reader feel clever relative to Watson while Holmes stays mythic.
Archie Goodwin is the device perfected as voice: the companion becomes the book's stylistic engine, not just its camera.
Hastings shows the device's failure mode: a Watson with no interiority of his own flattens into a walking notebook.

entries.name: The Drawing-Room Reveal
entries.description: Gather the suspects; solve in public; watch the faces.

examples.text: Poirot's assemblies work because the gathering itself applies pressure: the reveal is an interrogation staged as a performance.
Stages the ceremony knowingly and plays it straight anyway — proof the form survives its own parody when the underlying deductions are sound.
The reveal as formula furniture: weekly assemblies where the confession arrives on schedule, teaching the ceremony without the earned deduction beneath it.

entries.name: Disguise and Misdirected Identity
entries.description: The person you're looking at is not who you think.

examples.text: Doyle runs disguise in both directions: Holmes's costumes succeed until Irene Adler answers with her own — the device examined, not just used.
Disguise sustained until it replaces the self: identity theft as psychological process rather than trick, the trope's deepest treatment.
Disguise as gag: reveals played for laughs spend the device's tension faster than it accrues.

entries.name: The Criminal Mastermind
entries.description: The intelligence on the other side of the board.

examples.text: Moriarty invented the archetype in a handful of pages: the mastermind works best as gravity — felt everywhere, seen almost never.
Lecter refines it: the mastermind as oracle, whose help costs more than opposition would.
The inflation failure mode: a mastermind so omnipotent that plot logic dissolves — when everything is planned, nothing is earned.

entries.name: The Wrongly Accused
entries.description: Innocent, hunted, and forced to solve the crime themselves.

examples.text: Hitchcock's double-hunt template: pursued by police and villains at once, the fugitive investigates because standing still means capture.
The form's modern summit: pursuit as procedure on both sides, with the pursuer's gradual conversion as the real plot.
The interior version: accused, not fleeing — the machinery of prosecution experienced from the defendant's chair, with the genre's best-kept final reveal.

entries.name: The Cipher
entries.description: The coded message: meaning locked, plot as key.

examples.work: The Adventure of the Dancing Men
examples.text: The genre's model cipher: simple enough to solve alongside Holmes, deadly enough to matter — and the decoding is shown, not asserted.
The honest counterweight: real ciphers, partial solutions, and the corrosive cost of codes that never fully open.
Ciphers as breadcrumb dispenser: each puzzle exists to emit the next location, decorative difficulty with the solving outsourced to exposition.

entries.name: The Gentleman Thief
entries.description: Crime with manners: the charming professional the reader roots for.

examples.text: Raffles founded the type and kept the ledger honest: the charm is real, and so, quietly, is the parasitism it decorates.
Leblanc's thief outwits detectives with theatrical generosity — the continental pole of the type, style as morality.
The retired version: reputation as trap, romance as tension, and theft refined to pure elegance — the trope at its most weightless and most durable.

entries.name: The Copycat Crime
entries.description: A crime imitating a crime — and the gap between original and copy as evidence.

examples.text: The inversion that defines the trope's ceiling: the pattern exists to hide the one murder that matters — imitation as camouflage.
The literal treatment: a killer performing famous murders, with the expert who studies them forced to read her own syllabus as threat.
Copycatting industrialized into cult logistics: escalation replaces coherence, and the imitation premise consumes its own plausibility.

entries.name: The Cold Case Reopened
entries.description: Old evidence, new eyes: the past refusing to stay filed.

examples.text: The ultimate cold case — five centuries cold — solved from a hospital bed with documents alone: pure reasoning as narrative engine.
The detective's own childhood case shadows the new one: reopening as psychological excavation, with the cold file inside the investigator.
Seventeen years between the case and its truth: the reopening structure braided with the cost of the years themselves.

entries.name: The Detective in Peril
entries.description: The investigator becomes the target — proximity to truth priced in danger.

examples.text: Marlowe drugged, beaten, and ambushed as standard operating cost: peril as the hardboiled form's tax on knowledge.
The terminal version: the detective's death as the price of victory — and the genre's most famous resurrection debt.
The formula version: the killer targets the detective because the series needs personal stakes, a shortcut that replaces investigation with jeopardy.

entries.name: The Amateur Who Outperforms the Police
entries.description: The civilian lens that sees what the badge misses.

examples.text: The consulting detective defined against Scotland Yard: Lestrade is competent enough that Holmes's edge reads as method, not authorial favoritism.
Marple's village omniscience beats procedure honestly: her data set (human nature, locally observed) is one the police genuinely lack.
The failure mode YA craft warns against: adults exist only to be wrong, so the amateurs' victories are bought with the world's competence.

entries.name: The Second Murder
entries.description: Killing to cover a killing: the crime that compounds.

examples.text: The cover-killings escalate on a timetable the reader can reconstruct: each new death is the first death's logic extending itself.
Compounding as complete structure: one shabby crime metastasizing through incompetence — the second murder as the form's tragic engine.
The spiral interiorized: each killing purchases temporary safety at permanent moral cost, priced scene by scene.

entries.name: The Faked Death
entries.description: The corpse that wasn't: death as disguise.

examples.work: The Adventure of the Empty House
examples.text: The genre's founding resurrection: Holmes's return set the rules — a faked death must be planted fairly and explained completely.
The device weaponized: a faked death engineered as narrative, with the fraud's meticulousness itself the characterization.
The refusal to resolve: multiple joke explanations instead of one honest one — spending reader trust to dodge the debt the trope incurs.

entries.name: Twins and Doubles
entries.description: Two faces, one identity — the device the Golden Age had to ban.

examples.text: The twin as total structural solution, planted with scrupulous fairness: the banned device redeemed by making the concealment itself the theme.
Doubles at horror scale: the crime-thriller device expanded into social metaphor while keeping its identity-swap mechanics honest.
Twin-swap as premise treadmill: the device generates complications faster than plausibility can service them. Knox banned twins for a reason; this is the reason.

entries.name: The Poison Pen
entries.description: Anonymous letters: community intimacy turned toxic.

examples.text: Christie's own favorite: the letters as misdirection layer, with the village's guilty consciences doing the amplification.
Drawn from a real 1920s case: the trope's class and gender machinery made explicit — who is believed, and why, is the whole engine.
Poison-pen plots as village-formula filler: the letters arrive on schedule, the community machinery the device depends on reduced to backdrop.

entries.name: The Long Con
entries.description: The extended deception: trust cultivated as a crop.

examples.text: The architecture standard: the con's stages formalized, the mark's psychology respected, and the audience conned along with him — fairly.
The con turned inward: the grifter as mark, with the long deception braided into genuine relationship — the trope's emotional ceiling.
Con layers stacked until none bear weight: when everything might be part of the con, the reveal has nothing solid to land on.

entries.name: The Inside Job
entries.description: The betrayal of access: the crime only an insider could commit.

examples.text: The heist that runs on institutional knowledge — of bank procedure, police response, and media rhythm — with the "inside" revealed as historical rather than personnel.
Access inherited rather than held: the notebook as insider knowledge passed across a death, and the job's real inside track is political.
Staff knowledge as caper decal: the building's workers supply access without the film dramatizing what insiders actually know — the trope's premise asserted, not earned.

entries.name: The Mole
entries.description: The enemy at the next desk: institutional trust as the crime scene.

examples.text: The mole hunt perfected: suspicion distributed across four fully-realized candidates, the investigation conducted through files and memory, and the betrayal priced in marriages as well as operations. The form's masterpiece.
Symmetrical moles hunting each other: the trope doubled into a hall of mirrors, with cellphone-era pacing replacing le Carré's archival patience.
The mole-of-the-season formula: institutional betrayal as renewable twist, which trains the audience to trust no character investment.

entries.name: The Femme Fatale
entries.description: Desire as weapon; the seduction that is also the plot.

examples.text: Brigid O'Shaughnessy is the template: every version of her story a fresh con, with Spade's refusal the genre's coldest moral line.
Phyllis runs the noir engine in its purest form: the fatale as catalyst for a man's self-chosen fall — he talks himself into it; she just opens the door.
The type as spectacle: danger aestheticized past agency, teaching the surface of the trope while discarding the interiority that makes it work.

entries.name: The Corrupt Institution
entries.description: The rot is structural: when the system itself is the antagonist.

examples.text: Corruption as ecosystem: three cops, three compromises, one department — the institution examined through everyone it shapes.
The documentary pole: institutional corruption mapped from inside by the officer who refused it, at documented personal cost.
The maximal treatment: corruption as emergent property of institutional incentives rather than individual villainy — the trope elevated to sociology.

entries.name: The Serial Killer's Signature
entries.description: The pattern as text: crime scenes that communicate.

examples.text: The origin of the modern treatment: signature as psychological handwriting, read by an investigator whose gift for reading it is a wound.
Signature as sermon: the pattern is the killer's argument, and the investigators' interpretation of it is the film's structure.
Signature inflated to franchise: the pattern generates content rather than meaning, demonstrating the trope's exhaustion mode.

entries.name: The Hostage Standoff
entries.description: The sealed room with the world watching: negotiation as drama.

examples.text: The standoff as pressure-cooker character study: the crime dissolves into its human circumstances in real time, with the crowd as chorus.

examples.work: The Taking of Pelham One Two Three
examples.text: The procedural pole: negotiation as chess between professionals, with the city's institutional machinery as the board.
The standoff as staged performance: the siege engineered by the takers to run exactly as police procedure predicts — the negotiation playbook weaponized against its authors.

entries.name: The Vanished Witness
entries.description: The person who saw — gone, hidden, or erased.

examples.text: The protection structure at its best: the witness's world (Amish country) becomes the story, and protecting him remakes the protector.
Witness protection as noir punchline: survival delivered as living death — "an average nobody" — the trope's bleakest honest ending.
Protection as action pretext: the witness reduced to a package in transit, the trope's machinery used without any of its meaning.

entries.name: The Ticking Clock
entries.description: The fixed deadline that converts investigation into race.

examples.text: The clock given a face: Catherine alive in the pit makes the deadline a person, and every procedural delay an act of violence.
The clock as format: real-time structure makes the deadline the show's physics rather than a plot device — the trope industrialized.
Real-time as gimmick: the clock runs but nothing accumulates, proof the device needs stakes attached to the seconds.

entries.name: The Cat-and-Mouse Game
entries.description: Hunter and hunted, aware of each other, converging.

examples.text: The engineering standard: dual procedurals — assassin's preparation, detective's pursuit — converging for four hundred pages on a target the reader knows survives, and gripping anyway. Suspense built entirely from process.
The duet made explicit: professional respect across the table, with both men's competence the engine and their symmetry the theme.
Mutual obsession as premise decays into repetition: when neither cat nor mouse may win, the game loses its geometry.

entries.name: The Unreliable Narrator
entries.description: The account is the crime scene: narration you can't trust.

examples.text: POV identity concealment executed with total fairness: the structure hides the killer in plain grammatical sight.
The investigation that is itself the delusion: every clue honest twice — once for the case, once for the truth.
The device assembled from its own hits: unreliability as checklist (wine, pills, grief) rather than engineered perception.

entries.name: Gaslighting
entries.description: The engineered doubt: making the victim distrust their own mind.

examples.text: The source of the term: the dimming lights, the moved objects, the husband's patient project — the mechanism documented step by step.
Ambient gaslighting by a dead woman's household: no single villain required when architecture, staff, and silence collaborate.
Abuse depicted without the doubt machinery: the victim knows the truth throughout, which is horror but not gaslight — the term misapplied teaches the trope wrong.

entries.name: In Over Their Head
entries.description: The ordinary person who touches the criminal world and can't let go.

examples.text: Moss takes the money in full knowledge, and the novel prices that one comprehensible choice at everything — the trope at maximum consequence.
The graduate student inherited into his brother's world: expertise (running, history) repurposed as survival equipment.
The recruit who audits his own gilded cage: discovery, entrapment, and the amateur's leverage — the corporate version of the template.

entries.name: The Chase
entries.description: Pursuit as set piece and structure.

examples.text: The chase as procedural centerpiece: obsession given velocity, with the pursuit's recklessness characterizing the pursuer.
The template modern car chases descend from: geography coherent, stakes personal, engine noise as score.
Pursuit as franchise obligation: chases that neither reveal character nor alter the situation — motion without story.

entries.name: The Trap
entries.description: The engineered situation with one designed exit — or none.

examples.work: The Adventure of the Speckled Band
examples.text: The detective springs the villain's own mechanism back on him: the trap reversed as poetic verdict.
Traps nested in traps, metafictionally: a thriller about writing thrillers where every plan is somebody's script.
The trap as spectacle divorced from detection: mechanism worship, with the investigative frame vestigial.

entries.name: The Stalker
entries.description: The watcher: obsession as slow-motion threat.

examples.text: The captor-fan: obsession domesticated into caretaking, with the victim's craft (writing) as both cause and weapon.
The escalation ladder documented: from encounter to siege in credible increments, each deniable until it isn't.
The stalker's charming interiority as deliberate trap for the audience: satire that indicts the viewer's complicity with romantic framing.

entries.name: The Home Invasion
entries.description: The safe place breached: threat where safety was assumed.

examples.text: The template: fugitives in the family home, with the household's ordinary geography converted room by room into hostage terrain.
The anti-version: the invasion staged to indict the audience's appetite for it — the trope interrogating its own consumers.
Dread without meaning: "because you were home" abandons motive and with it everything the genre could say about the violation.

entries.name: The Kidnapping and the Ransom Exchange
entries.description: The abduction, the demand, and the drop: crime as negotiation.

examples.text: Kurosawa's kidnapping procedural is the trope's complete statement: the wrong child taken, the ransom as moral test, the drop as set piece, and the investigation as class portrait. Every subsequent ransom story is working in its shadow.
The abduction examined until every party's motive curdles: the recovery question — returned to what? — as the real mystery.
The negotiation professionalized but the story outsourced to romance: the K&R detail convinces, the plot around it doesn't.

entries.name: The Bomb Under the Table
entries.description: Hitchcock's principle embodied: the audience knows, the characters don't.

examples.text: The origin and the cautionary tale at once: Hitchcock detonated the bus bomb, regretted it publicly, and the lesson — suspense is a promise you keep, not spend — entered the craft canon.
The opening crane shot: one unbroken take with the bomb in the trunk — the principle perfected as choreography.
The principle industrialized honestly: the bomb's rules stated, kept, and escalated — high-concept suspense that plays fair to the last frame.

entries.name: The Vanishing Spouse
entries.description: The person who shared your bed, gone — and the marriage becomes the evidence.

examples.text: The definitive modern treatment: the vanished wife as author of the vanishing, and the marriage's competing narratives as the true crime scene.
The Dutch original: the answer to "what happened" delivered as the genre's most pitiless ending — curiosity itself weaponized.
Disappearance as twist-delivery mechanism: reveals stacked until the marriage at the center has no consistent reality to betray.

entries.name: The Amnesiac Protagonist
entries.description: The self as mystery: investigation turned inward.

examples.text: The template: skills intact, identity gone, so competence itself becomes the clue trail — who trains a man to do this?
Amnesia as structure: the backwards architecture forces the audience into the protagonist's condition — the trope's formal summit.
The daily reset serves the twist more than the character: premise maintenance visibly strains, and the machinery shows through the dread.

entries.name: Mistaken Identity
entries.description: The wrong man, taken for someone else — and the error has momentum.

examples.text: The pure engine: an identity that never existed, pursued across a continent — the trope run at maximum velocity and wit.
The trope as comedy without breaking its mechanics: the wrong Lebowski absorbs a noir plot that works whether he understands it or not.
Mistaken identity as franchise bait: reveals contradict, stakes float free, and the error at the center has no logic to sustain pursuit — the trope with its engine removed.

entries.name: The Deadly Inheritance
entries.description: The will, the fortune, and the motive it prints.

examples.text: The inheritance plot dressed as a curse: the entail is the motive, the legend is the method, and the moor is the misdirection.
The will-reading template: heirs gathered at midnight, fortunes contingent on sanity — the scene every inheritance mystery restages.
The YA expression: the puzzle-will as invitation rather than motive, converting the trope's dread into agency — instructive on how audience changes the same machinery.

entries.name: Cut Off
entries.description: No phone, no help, no way out: isolation as pressure.

examples.text: Open ocean as the perfect sealed room: three people, two boats, and physics as the only law available.
The inversion: sealed in rather than cut off, with safety and trap revealed as the same architecture.
Isolation asserted but porous: the ship's cut-off status flickers as the plot requires, and the pressure leaks with it.

entries.name: The Sole Survivor
entries.description: The one who lived: testimony, trauma, and the account no one can check.

examples.text: The survivor's account as con: the trope's epistemology weaponized — the only witness is the author of the story we just watched.
Survival as lifelong evidence: the boy who came back carries the crime forward twenty-five years — the trope as wound rather than testimony.
The escapee as plot token: survival grants the heroine investigative standing the book then undervalues — testimony subordinated to the hunt's mechanics.

entries.name: The Body That Disappears
entries.description: The corpse — or witness — that was there, and isn't.

examples.text: The person-not-body variant: a witness gaslit by an entire train — the disappearance denied is scarier than the disappearance.
The inversion as comedy: a corpse that won't stay buried, logistics as farce — proof the trope's machinery runs in any tonal register.
The corpse as pure prop: disposal logistics played for gag physics with every real consequence — decomposition, discovery, grief — waved away; the trope's machinery with all the meaning drained.

entries.name: The Perfect Murder's Flaw
entries.description: The flawless plan, and the one thing it couldn't control.

examples.text: The criss-cross scheme's flaw is structural: the perfect plan requires a partner, and the partner is a person.
The single material slip — the latchkey — as the whole endgame: the plan reconstructed backwards through one object.
The format built entirely on the flaw: every episode a perfect murder and the one thread that unravels it — the trope as series engine, honestly run for decades.

entries.name: The Blackmailer
entries.description: The secret as commodity; the payment that never ends.

examples.work: The Adventure of Charles Augustus Milverton
examples.text: The master blackmailer as the one criminal Holmes despises: the story where the detective burgles, and the genre's ethics bend around a worse crime than theft.
The victim's POV: Hitchcock's first sound film runs the pressure from inside — the blackmailed as protagonist, guilt compounding the extortion.
The leverage economy at full noir wattage: the columnist and the press agent trading reputations as currency — blackmail as an ecosystem rather than a single villain's scheme.

entries.name: The Double Cross
entries.description: The betrayal among criminals: no honor, only leverage.

examples.text: The heist double-crosses cascading in nonlinear time: Kubrick's racetrack job as a study in how betrayal propagates through a plan.
The cross as structure: aftermath-first architecture, with the betrayal reconstructed rather than witnessed.
Crosses stacked for titillation: each reversal cheapens the last until the credits-sequence reveals read as admission the plot never cohered.

entries.name: The Getaway
entries.description: After the job: flight as its own discipline.

examples.text: Thompson's brutal logistics of flight: the escape as grinding, paranoid labor — the trope stripped of glamour down to its transactional bones.
The driver's code as characterization: five minutes either side, and the getaway as the one domain where the protagonist is articulate.
The getaway choreographed to score: technique as joy, with the trope's kinetics foregrounded and its costs still honestly billed.

entries.name: Dead Drops and Tradecraft
entries.description: The spy's grammar: procedure as language, discipline as survival.

examples.work: The Spy Who Came in from the Cold
examples.text: Tradecraft as moral machinery: every procedure exists to spend people efficiently, and the novel prices the spending.
The exchange as procedure: negotiation, protocol, and the bridge itself — tradecraft rendered as patient, humane craft.
Tradecraft as spectacle: the gadget replaces the discipline, teaching the surface of procedure without its logic or cost.

entries.name: The Honey Trap
entries.description: Seduction as tasking: intimacy weaponized by institutions.

examples.text: The deepest treatment: an actress recruited to live a fabricated love, with the trap's psychic cost to the operator as the subject.
The trap as plot spine, run in both directions: the lure knowingly deployed against the man trained to expect it.
Trap training as lurid spectacle: the institutional machinery convinces, but the camera lingers where the argument should be.

entries.name: The Sleeper Agent
entries.description: The enemy who has been your neighbor for years.

examples.text: The sleeper as horror of the self: the agent who doesn't know he's the weapon — the trope fused with its own psychology.
Sleeper domesticity as the entire premise: the marriage is the cover and the cover is the marriage — the trope's contradictions run for six patient seasons.
Sleeper reveals stacked into incoherence: each activation contradicts the last, and the premise's power — the long patience — is spent on velocity.

entries.name: The Defector
entries.description: The walk-in: the enemy who wants to change sides, and the question of belief.

examples.text: Defection as procedural set piece: the entire apparatus of two navies bent around one man's intention, which must be deduced from maneuvers.
The walk-in handled by an amateur: Penkovsky's real case run through an ordinary salesman — the defector trope at human scale, costs included.
The inversion: the "defector" hunt is a manufactured frame, and the man leading the search is its target — the trope's belief-question (is the walk-in real?) turned inside out.

entries.name: The Safe House
entries.description: The temporary refuge — safe exactly until it isn't.

examples.text: The house full of fugitives as sustained dread: safety as performance that must be maintained daily, drawn from the documented case.
Safe houses that are never safe: each refuge more provisional than the last, paranoia compounding as the operation's true product.
The title as the whole idea: breached for action within minutes, the trope used as a set rather than a state of mind.

entries.name: The Burned Spy
entries.description: Disavowed: the operative the institution erased.

examples.text: The retired spy recalled: the burn as institutional amnesia, with the discarded man's memory the one archive the Circus can't delete.
The premise serialized honestly: competence in exile, with the burned spy's tradecraft repurposed for small justice while the arc digs at who burned him.
Betrayal as fight-scene delivery system: the burn exists to schedule combat, and the institutional questions it raises go unasked.

entries.name: The Mismatched Partners
entries.description: Two incompatible cops, one case: friction as engine.

examples.text: The template refined to essentials: the suicidal wild card and the family man, with the mismatch itself doing the character work between set pieces.
The pairing as comic engine that still honors the case: incompetence and brutality complementing into accidental competence.
Chemistry over case: the mismatch generates banter but the investigation is a rumor — the trope reduced to casting.

entries.name: The Rookie and the Veteran
entries.description: Experience and innocence sharing a car: the worldview debate on wheels.

examples.text: The pairing as philosophical argument: Somerset's exhausted erudition against Mills's furious optimism, with the case as the debate's evidence.
The inversion: the veteran as corruptor, one shift as the whole syllabus — the mentorship trope run as seduction and trap.
The partnership without a corruption arc: two patrol officers whose bond is the subject — the pairing trope run on loyalty and daily procedure rather than mentor-betrayal.

entries.name: The Detective's Damage
entries.description: The wound that makes them good at this and bad at everything else.

examples.text: Rebus arrives damaged from the start — army, marriage, faith — and the series spends decades honestly compounding rather than resetting it.
Harry Hole's alcoholism priced correctly: the brilliance and the relapses belong to the same man, and cases are lost, not just anguished over.
Damage inflated to superpower: the torment licenses rule-breaking that always works — the wound as decoration rather than cost.

entries.name: The Last Case Before Retirement
entries.description: The countdown calendar on the desk: one more case, then out.

examples.text: The trope as elegy: Bell's retirement is the book's argument — the country has outrun the sheriff's comprehension, and leaving is the only honest verdict.
The parody that understands the machinery: every retirement-and-transfer beat inventoried lovingly and then played for keeps.
The criminal's mirror of the trope: the aging robber who can't retire because the work is the self — desistance (Psychology 20) examined from the other side of the badge.

entries.name: The Detective Off the Books
entries.description: Badge pulled, case continued: investigation without authority.

examples.text: The badge-toss codified: the film honestly frames the cost — the off-book detective gets results by becoming the thing the rules existed to prevent.
Jurisdiction zeroed out entirely: the detective as unauthorized guest, with charm as his only warrant.
Suspension as institutional weapon: Tennison worked out of the building by politics rather than misconduct — the off-book state imposed, not chosen, and gendered.

entries.name: The Jurisdiction Fight
entries.description: Feds versus locals: the case as territory.

examples.text: The FBI takeover as both plot mechanism and satire: procedure followed perfectly into catastrophe while the local improviser is written off.
Four jurisdictions strangling one case: the documented reality — evidence unshared, letters crossing, the killer profiting from org charts.
The jurisdiction maze as the theme itself: tribal land, federal crime, county indifference — the gaps between authorities rendered as the reason victims go uncounted.

entries.name: Internal Affairs
entries.description: The police policing the police — and being hated for it.

examples.text: IA as chess: investigations of investigators nested three deep, with career leverage the actual currency.
The IA shadow as conscience externalized: the compromise spiral driven by what's about to be found.
IA as season-length siege warfare: the Strike Team investigated across years, with the audit itself corrupted by careerism — the watchdog examined as another institution.

entries.name: The Informant
entries.description: The snitch: information as survival economy.

examples.text: The informant's world from inside: small stakes, real fear, and the grubby arithmetic of trading names for time — no glamour, no mastermind, just the economy of the barely surviving. The genre's most honest book about informing, and its best dialogue.
Informing symmetrized: each side's rat hunting the other, with the information economy accelerated to cellphone speed.
The turn as the life's terminal transaction: informing not as betrayal of honor but as the last deal available.

entries.name: The Criminal Consultant
entries.description: Visiting the monster: expertise purchased with self-exposure.

examples.text: The original consultation: Graham visits Lecter to recover the mindset that broke him — the device's founding scene, quid pro quo already implicit.
The device perfected: Lecter's price is Clarice herself, making every consultation a mutual excavation.
The consultant running the show: the device stretched until the monster is the protagonist's handler — menace dissolved by dependence.

entries.name: Undercover In Too Deep
entries.description: The cover that becomes a life: identity as occupational hazard.

examples.text: The friendship that makes the job a betrayal in every direction: based on the documented case, with the handler's creed — "I'm not becoming like them, I am them" — as thesis.
The undercover ledger audited: each maintained cover costs a piece of the self, tallied in voiceover.
Immersion as vibe: the case dissolves into the lifestyle, and the film forgets which side of the trope it's dramatizing.

entries.name: The Anonymous Tip
entries.description: The unsigned message that moves the case — and the question of who benefits.

examples.text: The managed source as structure: Deep Throat's rationed guidance — confirm, never originate — is the tip trope at its most disciplined.
Tips triaged by institutional journalism: the trope embedded in process, where a tip is a lead to verify, not a revelation to trust.
The tip as the killer's taunt: Scorpio directing the investigation by message — the anonymous channel reversed into an instrument of control.

entries.name: The Interrogation Duel
entries.description: Two people, one table: the genre's chamber drama.

examples.text: The box as theater with legality as the net: interrogations as tactical performances where the audience is the eventual courtroom.
Tennison's interviews as double chess: suspect across the table, institutional sexism at her back — two duels in every session.
The room inverted: the suspect conducts, the interrogators respond — a single-scene masterclass in who actually holds the frame.

entries.name: Good Cop / Bad Cop
entries.description: The oldest routine in the building — worn, known, and still working.

examples.text: The routine as institutional furniture: worn honestly, acknowledged by suspects, and effective anyway — procedure as ritual.
The routine performed solo: one interrogator cycling both roles through charm and steel — the device compressed into a single performer.
The routine as pure joke: parody that documents the trope's exhaustion without finding anything underneath it.

entries.name: The Autopsy Scene
entries.description: The body as witness: the morgue as reading room.

examples.text: The ME as protagonist origin point: autopsy rendered as authored, procedural reading — the scene that launched the forensic-thriller wave.
The long-running standard: pathology as viewpoint, with the dead granted the narrative dignity of being evidence that talks.
The lab as oracle: the ME solving everything from tissue alone — the scene's authority inflated past what any table can tell.

entries.name: The Crime Board
entries.description: The string wall: an investigator's mind made visible.

examples.text: Carrie's wall as the trope's dual image: brilliance and breakdown in the same collage — the board as diagnosis of its maker.
The storage-unit board: seventeen years of obsession archived — the board as a life spent rather than a case solved.
The "Pepe Silvia" wall: the definitive parody diagnosis of board-brain — apophenia rendered as comedy, and quietly the best warning the device has.

entries.name: The Stakeout
entries.description: Watching and waiting: surveillance as patience and voyeurism.

examples.text: The stakeout examined as voyeurism: the watcher implicated, the watching itself put on trial while still delivering the thriller.
Surveillance as corrosion: the professional watcher dissolved by his own methods — the stakeout turned inward.
The premise as rom-com engine: tension optional, ethics unexamined — the trope as sitcom set.

entries.name: The Confession That Doesn't Fit
entries.description: Someone confessed — and the details are wrong.

examples.text: The coerced-confession problem documented in real time: interrogation footage as the genre's most disturbing primary source (see Psychology collection on false confessions).
The confession pressure machine dramatized: how process, exhaustion, and counsel's absence manufacture certainty the evidence doesn't hold.
The true confessor unbelieved: Grisham's variation — the guilty man confessing to save an innocent, and the system too committed to its verdict to listen.

entries.name: The Prison Visit
entries.description: The glass divider: conversation as the only available action.

examples.text: Client visits as the reveal's slow fuse: every session plants the performance the ending detonates.
The documentary pole: death-row visits as the practice of seeing clients as full persons — the scene's moral weight without genre machinery.
The visit as moral practice: the death-row conversations carrying the entire film — the glass-divider scene stretched to feature length and earning every minute.

entries.name: The Crew Assembly
entries.description: Getting the band together: each member a skill and a flaw.

examples.text: The recruiting montage codified: role-call as character economy — each specialist introduced by function and vanity in thirty seconds.
The crew of strangers: assembly without trust, where vetting each other is the first job and the real one.
Roles as personality decals: the specialist labels applied without the underlying competence being dramatized.

entries.name: The Fence
entries.description: The market for stolen goods: crime's commercial layer.

examples.text: Fagin as the ur-fence: the receiving economy and its grooming pipeline, documented before the genre had a name.
The fence/dealer economy as pressure engine: every object simultaneously collateral, debt, and escape plan.
The stolen-goods economy as farce network: every character a node in the moving of one diamond — the receiving trade rendered as the plot's connective tissue.

entries.name: The Fixer
entries.description: The one you call: competence in service of concealment.

examples.text: The Wolf as the cleaner set piece: competence porn played for comedy without deflating the stakes underneath.
The fixer's self-disgust as the entire film: "janitor" as job description and self-verdict.
Fixing as episodic content mill: the jobs blur, the costs reset weekly, and the premise's moral question dulls with use.

entries.name: The Don's Audience
entries.description: Power as etiquette: the ritual of asking the boss.

examples.text: The wedding-day audiences are the institution taught in one sequence: favors as currency, respect as procedure, justice privatized — the entire underworld's political economy rendered as etiquette. The trope's founding and terminal text at once.
The sit-down as ethics debate: audiences where the subject is always loyalty and the stakes are always personal.
The audience ritualized into fantasy: markers, tables, and protocol — the trope's stylization limit, coherent because the rules are kept.

entries.name: The Turf War
entries.description: Territory as economy: the map drawn in blood.

examples.text: The turf war misread: the old gangster prices the threat in familiar currency while the enemy plays a different game entirely.
Turf war generational: territory inherited by children, with documentary energy replacing genre romance.
The pre-modern version: turf as tribal identity, where the war precedes and produces the city's institutions.

entries.name: The Protection Racket
entries.description: Insurance you didn't ask for: extortion as small business.

examples.text: The racket as banality: no-show jobs and skimmed registers — organized crime rendered as middle management with violence in reserve.
The racket from below: the dockworker's-eye view, where the levy is taken from wages and the enforcement is neighbors.
The racket from the stoop: the neighborhood boy's double education — the protection economy as community fact, seductive and priced, seen at child's-eye level.

entries.name: The Laundering Front
entries.description: The car wash, the casino, the restaurant: dirty money becoming clean.

examples.text: Laundering as domestic logistics: the car wash purchase negotiated like any family business decision — the crime normalized by its paperwork.
Laundering as the premise itself: the mechanics foregrounded, with the launderer's expertise the thing every faction wants to own.
Forensic accounting as action pretext: the ledger work asserted rather than dramatized, a spreadsheet taped over a gun movie.

entries.name: The Hitman's Code
entries.description: Rules inside the unforgivable: professional ethics for killing.

examples.text: The code as monastic aesthetic: ritual, solitude, and procedure — the template every stylish assassin since has copied.
The code articulated and broken in one night: the professional's rationalizations tested against a witness who keeps asking why.
The code as branding: barcode and rules-of-engagement iconography with no ethical machinery underneath.

entries.name: One Last Job
entries.description: The retired criminal pulled back: the score that breaks the code.

examples.text: The discipline — walk away in thirty seconds — stated, honored, and finally broken: the last job as the self-betrayal the code existed to prevent.
The refusal as the entire drama: the job itself is almost nothing; the recruiting visit is the war.
The last job as retrieval quest: stakes applied as decals, the retirement never credible enough for its ending to mean anything.

entries.name: The Disposal Problem
entries.description: The body is the evidence: getting rid of it is its own plot.

examples.text: Disposal as friendship autopsy: the logistics are manageable; what the work does to the flatmates is not.
The woodchipper as the compounding crime's terminal image: disposal escalating in grotesquerie as the original plan's remains shrink.
The bathtub lesson: disposal as chemistry with consequences — the show's early thesis that this work has procedures, and ignoring them has floors.

entries.name: The Digital Trail
entries.description: Phones, metadata, search histories: the evidence everyone generates all day.

examples.work: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo
examples.text: Salander's intrusions established the modern investigative pairing: archival legwork plus digital access, each finding what the other can't.
The screen-life form: the entire investigation conducted through interfaces, with the trail as the mise-en-scène itself.
Digital forensics as technobabble magic: capabilities invented per scene, teaching a generation of writers exactly the wrong lessons about what devices record.

entries.name: The Podcast Investigation
entries.description: The mic as warrant: civilian investigation with an audience.

examples.text: The braided form's landmark: the podcast investigating a girl who narrates in parallel — the frame's limits and the audience's helplessness as the tragedy's instrument.
The trope as comedy with a real mystery spine: podcast conventions lovingly inventoried while the fair-play machinery underneath stays honest.
The podcast frame as prestige veneer: the show forgets its own format for episodes at a time, using the mic as set dressing.

entries.name: The Web Sleuths
entries.description: The crowd investigates: distributed attention, zero accountability.

examples.text: The documentary that interrogates its own sleuths: real amateurs who genuinely helped, examined alongside the mob dynamics that make the practice dangerous.
The mockumentary diagnosis: web-sleuth and true-crime grammar parodied so precisely it doubles as a craft manual.

examples.work: A Good Girl's Guide to Murder
examples.text: The YA expression: the sleuth as web-native, with the investigation's documentation (logs, interviews, maps) printed as the book's own apparatus.

entries.name: The Watcher State
entries.description: Cameras everywhere: surveillance as setting and threat.

examples.text: The analog pole: the surveillance state embodied in one listener, converted by what he hears — the watcher as the watched society's conscience.
The camera-pull as action grammar: satellite to street in one move, the state's eye rendered as kinetic spectacle with real paranoia underneath.

Surveillance omniscience as procedural magic: the all-seeing Machine dispenses cases weekly, teaching precisely wrong lessons about what surveillance systems can know — the CSI effect's signals-intelligence cousin.

entries.name: The Catfish
entries.description: The person on the other end does not exist.

examples.text: The documentary that named the trope: the reveal handled with unexpected mercy, establishing the form's real subject — loneliness on both ends of the wire.
Persona construction from the predator's side: the curated self as hunting equipment.
The reveal as weekly formula: the trope's emotional machinery flattened into a segment rundown.

entries.name: The Contested Recording
entries.description: The tape that should settle it — and doesn't.

examples.text: The audio recording parsed in court syllable by syllable: evidence that hardens and dissolves depending on who narrates it — evidentiary ambiguity as the film's engine.
CCTV as unreliable narrator: deepfake doubt weaponized, the genre's first sustained treatment of footage that lies.

The recording as reconstruction project: the sound man assembling the crime from audio and stills — the evidence contested not in court but in the making, with the ending pricing what the tape was worth.

entries.name: The Cold Hit
entries.description: DNA decades later: the past arrested by a database.

examples.work: I'll Be Gone in the Dark
examples.text: The genetic-genealogy resolution arriving after the author's death: the cold hit as vindication the book itself never got to contain.
Genealogy as weekly magic: the method's real constraints and privacy questions unasked, the breakthrough always on schedule.
An early, fully documented genetic-genealogy conviction taken through trial: the cold hit from database match to verdict, with the method's objections given their full day in court.

entries.name: The Performed Life
entries.description: The social feed as alibi, evidence, and mask.

examples.text: The mommy-vlog layer: performance and audience baked into the mystery's structure, with the vlogger narrating her own investigation to her followers.
Persona construction as pathology: the follower who builds a life from someone else's feed — the trope's psychological floor.
The social-media premise burned through twist churn: each episode's reveal contradicts the platform logic the last one established.

entries.name: The Framing Interview
entries.description: The story told across a table — and shaped by the telling.

examples.text: The interview frame weaponized: the entire narrative is testimony, and the teller's control of the frame is the twist.
The interviews as the investigation itself: no chases, no forensics — conversation as the entire methodology, drawn from the real Behavioral Science Unit's origins.
The dictaphone confession as frame: the story told to a machine and a friend — the interview structure fused with noir's confessional voice, the ending known and the telling still unbearable.

entries.name: The Found Documents
entries.description: The case assembled from paper: letters, files, statements.

examples.text: The founding evidentiary novel: multiple narrators deposed in sequence, truth assembled from partial, biased accounts — the structure detective fiction was built on.
The modern revival: the novel is the case file — emails, messages, transcripts — with the reader explicitly deputized as investigator.
The transcript variation: audio files transcribed with errors intact ("mist er" for "mister") — the document form's imperfections themselves carrying clues.

entries.name: The Narrator's Confession
entries.description: The teller did it: narration as the scene of the crime.

examples.text: The founding execution: the confession hidden in the telling's gaps, every omission technically honest.
The confession destabilized: a narrator who confesses constantly to crimes that may not have happened — the trope pushed until reliability itself is the subject.
The confessor as predator: Barbara's journal narrating "friendship" while documenting a campaign — the confession trope where what's confessed and what's revealed are different crimes.

entries.name: Multiple Witnesses, Multiple Truths
entries.description: The same event, incompatible accounts, no referee.

examples.text: The definitional text: four testimonies of one crime, none arbitrated, the epistemology of witness itself put on screen. The genre borrowed the film's name for the effect because no work has stated the problem better.
The marriage retold by each party until the fall is unknowable: the Rashomon problem run through a courtroom's demand for one answer.

The three-account structure with the truth chapter marked: the same events through knight, squire, and wife — the Rashomon device given a verdict, and the naming of it ("the truth") the film's whole argument.

entries.name: The Story Within the Story
entries.description: The manuscript that holds the clues.

examples.text: The modern standard: a complete Golden Age novel nested inside a contemporary mystery, each solving the other — metafiction with a fair-play conscience.
The stolen story as evidence and engine: the book inside the book is the crime, and publishing it is the confession.
The nested fiction as confession and crime at once: the book's final reveal converts the story we read into the narrator's restitution — the embedded narrative bearing the guilt.

entries.name: The Retrospective Narrator
entries.description: Looking back at the crime: memory as the unreliable archive.

examples.text: The murder announced in the prologue and the book as long confession: the whydunit perfected, with complicity as atmosphere and the narrator's seduction by the group re-enacted on the reader. The campus-crime template, unmatched since.
The retrospective narrator's guilt reshaping the account itself: the confession is the book, and the book is the crime's continuation.
Retrospect that never resolves: guilt examined for a lifetime and left standing — the trope's ambiguous pole.

entries.name: The Courtroom Frame
entries.description: The trial as the story's spine: evidence in, verdict out.

examples.text: The procedure-honest standard: the whole narrative organized as one case's preparation and trial, ambiguity preserved through the verdict.
The frame from the defendant's chair: the trial structures the book while the truth waits outside it.
The frame at military pitch: the reveal-on-the-stand earned by procedural groundwork — the "you can't handle the truth" eruption as the cross-examination trap sprung, not a gift.

entries.name: The Small Town With Secrets
entries.description: Everyone knows everyone; no one knows anything.

examples.text: The town as pathology map: one death opening every door, the trope's television apotheosis and its strangest expression.
Grief as communal exposure: the investigation matters less than what suspicion does to a town that must keep living together.
The detective inside the secrets: the investigator's own family in the evidence pile — the trope with no outside to stand on.

entries.name: The Missing Woman the Cameras Love
entries.description: Whose disappearance counts: the media machine as plot element.

examples.text: The media descent on a photogenic case, with the reporter protagonist herself part of the machine she documents.
The counter-trope: the women nobody reports — overdose deaths on one police district's rounds — and the sister who counts them anyway.
The syndrome as programming strategy: case selection by demographics, the machine running undisguised.

entries.name: The Perfect Family Facade
entries.description: The household as performance: what the neighbors never saw.

examples.text: The facade run as ensemble: school-gate performances cracking in parallel, with the violence behind one door implicating the audience of all of them.

examples.work: We Need to Talk About Kevin
examples.text: The facade examined from inside by the one who couldn't maintain it: maternal ambivalence as the story no one wants witnessed.
The facade cracked by twist schedule rather than observation: reveals arriving as programming beats, the household never real enough to hide anything.

entries.name: The Class-Divide Investigation
entries.description: Upstairs and downstairs know different things.

examples.text: Two suspect pools with separate epistemologies: the servants know everything and are asked nothing — the class structure as the mystery's architecture.
Class infiltration curdling into crime: the divide as the whole plot's physics, genre-adjacent and the apex of the theme.
Class predation as aesthetic: the mechanics of the con obscured by tableau, the ledger never legible enough to audit.

entries.name: The Outsider Detective
entries.description: Foreign to the community — which is exactly the point.

examples.work: In the Heat of the Night
examples.text: The outsider detective and the town's racism as the true case: every interview a confrontation the murder merely licenses.
The outsider as moral instrument: the investigation as staged audit of a family's — and a class's — conscience.
The imported detective under midnight sun: the outsider's authority eroding as the place's conditions dismantle him.

entries.name: The Imperfect Victim
entries.description: The dead had secrets too: victimology as revelation.

examples.text: Rosie Larsen's life disclosed in layers: each revelation re-sorting the suspect pool and re-indicting the mourners' assumptions.
The victim's household as moral quicksand: rescue and return meaning different things once the family is known.
Megan's layers disclosed in retrospect: the victim's secrets re-sorting reader judgment — the trope run inside the unreliable-witness structure, each revelation indicting an earlier assumption.

entries.name: The Wrongful Conviction Unraveled
entries.description: The system got it wrong — and fights the correction.

examples.text: The Central Park Five: the manufacturing of guilt dramatized stage by stage — interrogation, media, plea machinery — and the decades the correction cost.
The Walter McMillian case as anatomy of a wrongful conviction and the institutional immune response to its unraveling.
Grisham's nonfiction turn: conviction anatomy in a small Oklahoma town, the genre novelist auditing the real machinery.

entries.name: Everybody Did It
entries.description: The conspiracy of suspects: guilt distributed across the whole pool.

examples.text: The trope's founding and terminal case: collective guilt as collective verdict, with the detective's choice about justice as the real ending.
The village conspiracy played as action-comedy: the collective-guilt reveal staged with complete genre literacy — parody as second-best analysis.
The multiple-ending gag: collective guilt as farce mechanics — the trope's machinery displayed and played entirely for comedy, instructive as parody but teaching none of its discipline.

entries.name: The Guilty Investigator
entries.description: The hunt that leads home: the detective in the evidence.

examples.text: The investigation as self-discovery damnation: every lead a mirror, the case file a biography.
The hunt self-authored: the investigator manufacturing his own mystery to have one worth solving — the trope's bleakest mechanism.
The reveal as exhausted formula: the investigator-is-culprit twist arriving on schedule — the device's power spent by a decade of imitation, a marker of the trope's saturation point.

entries.name: The Unsolved Ending
entries.description: No answer comes: irresolution as the point.

examples.text: The ambiguous ending as national wound: the final look into the camera turns the unsolved case outward onto everyone — the trope's most devastating execution.
The unsolved as metaphysics: the disappearance never explained because explanation is the thing the book refuses on principle.
The childhood case left standing: famously divisive, deliberately so — the withheld answer as the detective's permanent condition.

entries.name: The Villain's Monologue
entries.description: The explanation the villain can't resist giving.

examples.text: The monologue earned as thesis: John Doe's cab speech is the film's argument delivered by its author — the trope at maximum legitimacy.
The inversion that ended the trope's innocence: the plan explained only after it's too late to stop — "I did it thirty-five minutes ago."
The cautionary classic: the monologue as delay mechanism the hero exploits — the trope teaching its own vulnerability.

entries.name: The False Solution
entries.description: The convincing answer that comes before the right one.

examples.text: The trope as entire structure: six investigators, six complete solutions, each demolished by the next — the genre's own critique of its confidence.
The nested false solution: the manuscript's wrong answer engineered to expose the frame story's right one.
The pattern as false solution: the serial-killer reading of the crimes is itself the misdirection — the wrong theory built for the police and reader alike, then collapsed into the single true motive.

entries.name: The Posthumous Reveal
entries.description: The dead get the last word: wills, letters, and recordings from the grave.

examples.text: The will-game puppeteer: the dead man running the plot from inside his own testament — the YA/MG classic every inheritance-puzzle descends from.
The deathbed confession as structure: the truth rationed by a dying teller who controls the schedule of her own reveal.
The dead woman's contingency: evidence preserved and delivered on a timer — the posthumous reveal as planned counterattack rather than confession, the trope weaponized by its victim.

entries.name: Fingerprinting
entries.description: The oldest identity science: friction-ridge patterns, unique and permanent — but matching is human judgment, not machine certainty, and partial or smudged latents produce real disputes.

examples.text: Freeman's Thorndyke debates a forged fingerprint when the science was brand new: the first fictional cross-examination of the technique's infallibility myth, still instructive.
The instant database match: AFIS returns candidates for human examiners, not flashing verdicts — the procedural shortcut that rewrote public expectations wrongly.

entries.name: DNA Profiling
entries.description: The gold standard since the late 1980s — with real constraints: degraded samples, mixtures, transfer (your DNA travels without you), and lab backlogs measured in months.

examples.text: Wambaugh's account of the Colin Pitchfork case: the first DNA manhunt, complete with the world's first mass screening and the proxy scam that nearly beat it. The science's debut under real investigative pressure — the foundational text for writing DNA honestly.
Results in minutes, mixtures untangled by montage: the turnaround fantasy that makes every honest lab timeline read as a plot hole to trained-wrong audiences.

entries.name: Forensic Genetic Genealogy
entries.description: The 2018 revolution: unknown DNA matched to distant relatives via consumer databases, then family trees built down to a suspect. Powerful, slow, and privacy-contested.

examples.work: I'll Be Gone in the Dark
examples.text: The Golden State Killer's arrest — by exactly this method, weeks after publication — made the book the technique's accidental monument; the afterword era is the case study.
The Talbott case: genetic genealogy's first jury conviction, documented from cold case to courtroom with the method's mechanics and objections both on the record.

entries.name: Toxicology
entries.description: Poisons in tissue: what was taken, how much, and — hardest — whether it killed. Screening finds the known; the exotic must be suspected before it's found.

examples.text: Blum's Jazz Age chronicle of Norris and Gettler inventing American forensic toxicology poison by poison: the discipline's origin story with case detail writers can mine for decades.
Sayers builds the fair-play spine from arsenic mechanics — tolerance, timing, and the egg — chemistry as clue, honestly planted.

entries.name: Ballistics & Firearms Examination
entries.description: Matching bullets and casings to weapons by toolmarks — a comparison discipline whose "match" language has been formally softened; class evidence, not fingerprints for guns.

examples.text: The shotgun evidence chain from crime scene to confession: physical evidence as the documentary spine of the form's founding book.
The bullet fragment controversy: chain-of-custody and contamination disputes shown as the real battlefield — where ballistics cases are actually won and lost.

entries.name: Bloodstain Pattern Analysis
entries.description: Reading spatter for position, weapon, and sequence — a discipline whose scientific footing the 2009 NAS report found seriously wanting; write it as contested, because it is.

examples.text: BPA's reliability crisis on camera: dueling experts reading the same stairwell into opposite stories — the honest state of the field, filmed.
The analyst as superhero: spatter yielding cinematic certainty nightly — the discipline's confidence inflated exactly as the real courts were deflating it.

entries.name: Trace Evidence
entries.description: Fibers, hairs, soil, glass: the small transfers that place people at scenes. Class evidence again — a carpet fiber narrows the world, it doesn't name a name.

examples.text: Holmes's monographs on tobacco ash and mud: the fictional origin of trace obsession, written a decade before Locard formalized the principle.
McDermid's discipline-by-discipline survey, written by a crime novelist for exactly this use: the working writer's honest reference.

entries.name: Forensic Entomology
entries.description: Insect succession as clock: blowfly colonization timelines estimate postmortem interval across days and weeks — weather-dependent, and expressed in ranges, not timestamps.

examples.text: Erzinçlioğlu's casebook: a working forensic entomologist on real investigations — the method's genuine power and genuine humility in the practitioner's own voice.
Bug-clock precision to the hour: the ranges collapsed for plot convenience, teaching the technique's confidence without its error bars.

entries.name: Time of Death Estimation
entries.description: Algor, livor, rigor — cooling, settling, stiffening — plus stomach contents and entomology: converging estimates with wide, honest ranges that narrow only in fiction.

examples.text: Scarpetta's estimates carry their uncertainty into the plot: investigation proceeds on ranges, and the ranges matter — the honest version, dramatized.
"Between 9:15 and 9:40": the impossible precision that exists so alibis can be checked against it — the trope's most common quiet cheat.

entries.name: The Autopsy
entries.description: Cause (the injury or disease), manner (homicide, suicide, accident, natural, undetermined), mechanism: the postmortem's real vocabulary, with "undetermined" a legitimate and common verdict.

examples.text: Melinek's two years as a New York ME — 262 autopsies including 9/11 — the insider text: procedure, gallows humor, and the emotional ledger, all accurate.
The procedure rendered step by honest step until the findings break reality: proof that accuracy amplifies rather than limits dread.

entries.name: Forensic Odontology
entries.description: Dental ID of remains: solid. Bite-mark matching on skin: near-discredited — a headline casualty of the forensic-science reckoning. The gap between those two sentences is the card.

examples.text: The Bundy conviction's famous bite-mark evidence: the technique's most celebrated courtroom win, now its most instructive cautionary study — Rule's account preserves the certainty of the moment.
Junk-science identification in a wrongful conviction: Grisham documents what the same categories of confidence did to Ron Williamson.

entries.name: Forensic Anthropology
entries.description: The skeleton's testimony: age, sex, stature, ancestry (contested), trauma timing — from bone alone. Slow, rigorous, and best on the long-dead.

examples.text: Reichs writing her own profession: the bone lab's actual procedures carried into fiction with practitioner-grade fidelity — the field's authentic novelistic voice.
Koff's forensic anthropology at genocide scale — Rwanda, the Balkans: the discipline's gravest application, documented by a working scientist.

entries.name: Document Examination
entries.description: Handwriting attribution, ink and paper dating, alterations: genuine expertise with subjective edges — history's most famous forgeries fooled the examiners first.

examples.text: The Hitler Diaries fiasco: how authentication fails under pressure of wanting to believe — the discipline's essential cautionary epic.
Handwriting attribution as courtroom drama from a real 1920s case, with the era's certainty about it played both straight and skeptically.

entries.name: Forensic Accounting
entries.description: Following the money: ledgers, shells, and transaction trails. The dullest-sounding discipline convicts the most powerful defendants.

examples.text: Carreyrou unwinding Theranos: investigative accounting journalism as thriller — documents, whistleblowers, and the paper trail closing in.
The ledger work asserted, never dramatized: forensic accounting as backstory decal on an action film.

entries.name: Arson Investigation
entries.description: Fire science rebuilt itself after 1992 (NFPA 921): pour patterns, crazed glass, and "accelerant indicators" of the old school were largely myth. Pre-reform arson cases are a wrongful-conviction seam.

examples.text: The Willingham case: the old fire-reading mythology and its human cost, dramatized from the documented record.
"The fire talks": arson investigation as mysticism — gorgeous, influential, and precisely the folklore the field spent a decade purging.

entries.name: Gunshot Residue
entries.description: GSR: particles that say a gun went off nearby — transferable by handcuffs, police cars, and handshakes. Presence is suggestive; absence proves nothing.

examples.text: GSR handled with rare honesty: the evidence's ambiguity argued rather than asserted, transfer problems included.
GSR as binary guilt marker: positive equals shooter in forty minutes — the transfer literature waved off for verdict convenience.

entries.name: Serology
entries.description: Blood typing before DNA: ABO groups narrowed suspect pools for a century — class evidence that convicted when treated honestly and wrongly convicted when treated as identity.

examples.text: Holmes's debut scene is the invention of a hemoglobin test: detective fiction predicting serology's forensic use before the science had it.
The blood-type match played as identification: the era's standard overclaim, preserved in amber for study.

entries.name: Facial Reconstruction
entries.description: Rebuilding a face from a skull: tissue-depth data plus artistry. An identification lead-generator, not evidence — the face invites a name; other science must confirm it.

examples.text: The faceless corpses rebuilt as the novel's spine: reconstruction rendered as patient, political, and central — the technique's definitive fictional treatment.
The cold-case unit's reconstruction-and-appeal cycle: the technique in its honest procedural role, generating leads rather than verdicts.

entries.name: Audio Forensics
entries.description: Enhancement, voice comparison, authentication: real capabilities wrapped in the genre's favorite fantasy — "clean that up" has limits the waveform sets.

examples.text: Enhancement as obsession and error: the same tape re-read until its meaning inverts — the discipline's epistemology as tragedy.
The accidental recording reconstructed into evidence: audio forensics as protagonist skill, with the era's physical tape craft lovingly procedural.

entries.name: Digital Device Forensics
entries.description: Imaging, hash integrity, deleted-data recovery: real and powerful — but encryption is genuinely unbreakable in the movie sense, and "enhance" applies to nothing.

examples.text: Technically literate throughout: real tools, real techniques, real constraints — the standard proof that accuracy and drama are allies.
Two idiots, one keyboard: the canonical wrong-lesson scene — digital work as incantation, deservedly the genre's most mocked moment.

entries.name: Cell-Site Analysis
entries.description: Tower pings locate a phone to a sector, not a spot: coverage maps wobble, and drive-testing disputes fill hearings. Location evidence in ranges, like everything honest.

examples.text: The cell-tower evidence contested in public: the technique's assumptions audited episode by episode — the most influential demonstration of location evidence's real texture.
Real-time triangulation to the meter: the fantasy version that made honest sector testimony sound like equivocation to juries.

entries.name: Chemical Analysis
entries.description: Spectrometry and chromatography identify substances — drugs, accelerants, unknowns — with genuine authority. The lab's most solid ground, and the least dramatized.

examples.text: Method development as narrative: each chapter a substance, each substance a case — analysis dramatized through what it cost to invent.
Holmes the working chemist: the bench science rendered as character — the genre's founding portrait of analytical patience.

entries.name: Impression Evidence
entries.description: Footwear and tire marks: class evidence (make, model, wear) shading toward individual (cuts, gouges). Honest and underused — everyone walks in, everyone drives away.

examples.text: The cat's-paw boot sole: impression evidence as the documented, decisive link — quiet physical fact against the book's psychological expanse.
The tire-mark climax: courtroom-accurate, expert-driven, and beloved by actual forensic examiners — comedy carrying the discipline's honest logic.

entries.name: Locard's Exchange Principle
entries.description: Every contact leaves a trace — the field's founding axiom, and its honest fine print: traces transfer both ways, degrade, contaminate, and require someone to think of looking.

examples.text: McDermid's survey opens where the field does — with Locard — and keeps the axiom's limits attached to every chapter that follows.
The expert who leaves no trace: the show's premise requires its own protagonist's science to be wrong — Locard suspended for the lead, enforced for everyone else.

entries.name: Chain of Custody
entries.description: Every hand that touches evidence, logged: the paper trail that makes physical evidence admissible — and the seam defense attorneys attack first.

examples.text: The custody and contamination arguments that moved a verdict: the definitive documentary study of what happens when the log has gaps.
Evidence handled bare-handed, pocketed, and passed around weekly: the custody fiction that makes real suppression hearings incomprehensible to trained-wrong audiences.

entries.name: Crime Scene Protocol
entries.description: First officer, perimeter, scene log, one path in and out: the choreography that preserves a scene — or fails to in the first ten minutes.

examples.text: The scene as chaotic real estate: neighbors, brass, and weather all inside the tape — protocol as constant negotiation rather than checklist.
Lockdown and cross-contamination taken seriously in a town where every officer knows every witness: protocol under small-town pressure.

entries.name: The Canvass
entries.description: Door-to-door: the unglamorous engine that closes more cases than the lab does.

examples.text: The canvass grind with its community friction intact: doors that don't open for police, and why.
Shoe-leather rendered patiently: re-canvassing at different hours, the day-shift lie and the night-shift truth.

entries.name: The Search Warrant
entries.description: Probable cause on paper, scope limits in practice: the warrant defines what a search legally is — and what falls outside it is lost.

examples.text: Warrants cut, corners with them: the series prices every shortcut, making the paperwork's absence the long arc's evidence trail.
Warrantless everything, consequences none: the action-movie standard that erased the Fourth Amendment from a generation's genre grammar.

entries.name: Interrogation Law
entries.description: Miranda (US) and PACE (UK): rights, recording, and counsel — two different architectures, both routinely dramatized wrong.

examples.text: Miranda hollowed by process: rights recited and neutralized in the same hour — the legal architecture's failure mode, dramatized from the record.
PACE as drama engine: the tape running, counsel present, the caution verbatim — proof that procedure honestly kept makes interviews more tense, not less.

entries.name: The Reid Technique and Its Critics
entries.description: The dominant American interrogation method — minimization, theme development, the presumption of guilt — and the false-confession literature that grew in its shadow.

examples.text: Reid-style interrogations producing recanted confessions, shown at length: the method's machinery and its failure cases in the subjects' own recorded words.
The interview room as the entire set: technique, counter-technique, and the PEACE-model contrast with American practice, run as pure chamber drama.

entries.name: Eyewitness Identification
entries.description: Lineups, showups, and confidence statements: identification procedure reformed by DNA exonerations — sequential lineups, blind administration, confidence recorded at first ID.

examples.text: The definitive text: the misidentification, the exoneration, and the reconciliation, co-written by the witness and the man she wrongly identified.
Eyewitness certainty dismantled in deliberation: the glasses, the el-train, the seconds — the case against confidence, argued before the science existed.

entries.name: The Polygraph
entries.description: Inadmissible almost everywhere, used constantly anyway — as interrogation prop, employment gate, and plot device measuring stress, not truth.

examples.text: Alder's history of the machine: born from equal parts science and showmanship, institutionalized by exactly the forces that should have doubted it.
The polygraph beaten on-screen: the machine as security theater, defeated by a beta blocker and composure — its real epistemic status dramatized.

entries.name: Criminal Profiling
entries.description: Behavioral inference from crime scenes: genuinely useful for prioritization, persistently oversold as prediction — the validity literature is modest and the mythology is not.

examples.text: The BSU's origins dramatized with the uncertainty intact: profiling as hypothesis-building interviews, institutional skepticism included.
Profiles as magic spells: characteristics recited mid-episode with courtroom certainty — the mythology broadcast weekly at scale.

entries.name: Open-Source Investigation
entries.description: OSINT: geolocation from shadows, flight trackers, social scraping, archive diffing — the new investigative discipline built from public data.

examples.text: The methodology documented by its founders: MH17 and Skripal walked through step by verifiable step — the field's manual disguised as memoir.
OSINT as narrative form: a father's amateur open-source investigation conducted entirely on screens, its techniques real enough to teach.

entries.name: Cold-Case Methodology
entries.description: Re-reading, re-testing, re-interviewing: cold cases close through new science on old evidence, relationships that have expired, and fresh eyes on the original file.

examples.text: The linked-case grind across years and jurisdictions: databases, MO matching, and the cost of the original investigation's failures — method as redemption.
The flashback solve: cases closed by remembering harder — the method replaced by sentiment and a period soundtrack.

entries.name: The Murder Book
entries.description: The case file as institution: chronology, reports, photos, and the theory of the case — the document that outlives detectives and convicts decades later.

examples.work: Homicide: A Year on the Killing Streets
examples.text: Simon's year inside Baltimore's homicide unit: the board, the paperwork, the interrogation culture, the clearance-rate economy — the single most influential document of how investigation actually works, and the source DNA of the genre's two best TV series. If the collection kept one book, this is it.
The murder book treated with correct reverence: binders carried, guarded, and re-read — the file as the case's true protagonist.

entries.name: Victimology
entries.description: The victim's life as investigative map: routines, relationships, finances, and the last 24 hours — most homicides are solved in the victim's own address book.

examples.text: Rosie Larsen's life disclosed in investigative order: each stratum of the victim's world re-sorting the suspect pool — victimology as the season's architecture.
Victim-centered policing with rare moral weight: the victim's family inside the investigation's every decision, the case never abstracted from its harm.

entries.name: Timeline Reconstruction
entries.description: The chronology assembled from receipts, cameras, phones, and witnesses — where alibis live and die, and where the single unexplained gap is the case.

examples.text: Timeline puzzle mechanics as the whole game: the reconstruction run by the suspects themselves, every timestamp a trap.
